questions.description: The one song where even the uncle who sings off-key is allowed to join in.
questions.question: It's sung by candlelight on Christmas Eve, features a “holder Knabe im lockigen Haar” (lovely boy with curly hair), and exists in over 300 languages. Which song?
hints: It's a very calm, slow song.
In the song it's late, and everyone is asleep.
The title describes a night when not a sound can be heard.
questions.fun_fact: The song was first sung in 1818, accompanied by a guitar instead of an organ.

media.author: The U.S. Army

questions.description: The vacuum cleaner is putting in overtime again this January.
questions.question: What trickles onto the floor when the Christmas tree slowly dries out in January?
hints: It's green and very small.
If you step on it, it can prickle a little.
A sewing kit has some too, but these come from the tree.
questions.fun_fact: The Nordmann fir is Germany's favorite Christmas tree, partly because it stays green for a very long time.

media.credit: Steam Pipe Trunk Distribution Venue · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Steam Pipe Trunk Distribution Venue

questions.description: The only delivery service that always arrives on time but is never seen.
questions.question: It often has golden curls and wings, nobody sees it, and then a little bell rings. Why does the Christkind come on Christmas Eve?
hints: Children write it wish lists beforehand.
Afterward, there's more under the tree than before.
Think of packages tied with a bow.
questions.fun_fact: Martin Luther made the Christkind popular so that children would get presents at Christmas instead of on St. Nicholas Day.

media.credit: IIP Photo Archive from Washington, DC, USA · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: IIP Photo Archive from Washington, DC, USA

questions.description: The longest evening of the year, at least for anyone under ten.
questions.question: Complete: Heiligabend is the evening before …
hints: The next day, almost everyone has the day off.
On this day, the whole family often gets together.
In Germany, it's the first of two holidays in a row.
questions.fun_fact: In Germany, Christmas Eve is not a public holiday, so many shops are still open in the morning.

media.credit: Chris Olszewski · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Chris Olszewski

questions.description: Graffiti that even the building manager is happy to see.
questions.question: In early January, this chalk writing appears on many front doors. Why is “C+M+B” written there?
questions.answer: As a blessing for the house
wrong_answers: As a sign for the chimney sweep
As a receipt for the rent
As a note for the mail carrier
hints: Children dressed in royal robes write it on the door.
The letters stand for three Latin words.
“Christus mansionem benedicat” means: May Christ bless this house.
questions.fun_fact: C, M and B also match the names of the Three Kings: Caspar, Melchior and Balthasar.

media.author: 4028mdk09

questions.description: The little cone that turns any living room into a cozy smokehouse.

hints: They have no wick and burn without a flame.
You light only the tip, and then they slowly smolder.
They glow a bit like the stuff in a barbecue grill.
questions.fun_fact: With a Räuchermännchen, the smoke usually puffs out of the figure's mouth, as if it were smoking a pipe.

media.author: André Karwath aka Aka

questions.description: Round, soft and the secret stars of every gravy battle.
questions.question: You're at the Christmas table: roast goose, red cabbage and round Klöße (dumplings). What are the Klöße usually made from?
hints: It grows underground.
French fries are made from it too.
You dig them up in the field, often brown and lumpy.
questions.fun_fact: Klöße are so popular in Thuringia that there's even a dumpling museum there.

media.credit: Gerda Arendt · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Gerda Arendt

questions.description: A bird that comes to the Christmas table with a very full belly.
questions.question: The Christmas duck is roasted crisp in the oven, served with red cabbage and stuffed first. With what, classically?
hints: It's something fruity.
It grows in German gardens too.
In the fall it hangs on trees, and it also ends up in strudel.
questions.fun_fact: Mugwort often goes into the stuffing too, an herb said to make fatty poultry easier to digest.

media.credit: Tamorlan · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Tamorlan

questions.description: The day when the leftovers from the big feast get their moment in the spotlight.
questions.question: In Germany, what is December 26 called, the day many people visit relatives once more?
hints: Almost everyone has the day off.
It's the day after December 25.
It's already the second Christmas day off in a row.
questions.fun_fact: In church, December 26 is also called St. Stephen's Day, after Saint Stephen.

media.author: Unknown authorUnknown author

questions.description: The day boots suddenly matter more than homework.
questions.question: Nikolaus comes on December 6. How many little doors on the Advent calendar are open by then?
hints: You open the first door on December 1.
Exactly one more door opens each day.
Just count along: 1, 2, 3 …
questions.fun_fact: Nikolaus goes back to Bishop Nicholas of Myra, a town in what is now Turkey.

media.author: HerzenSterneBrezeln

questions.description: A saying so annoying that it's starting to crumble.

hints: The missing word is something baked.
It is small, round and crunchy.
People like to dunk it in milk.
questions.fun_fact: Nobody knows for sure where the saying comes from, but it has only been around since the 20th century.

media.author: Basile Morin

questions.description: A pocket you don't put your keys in, you sink your teeth into it.
questions.question: A Quarktasche from the bakery is filled with sweet quark. What is quark made from?
hints: It comes from the farm.
It comes from an animal.
Yogurt and cheese are made from it too.
questions.fun_fact: Quark forms when milk turns sour and thickens; the liquid left over is called whey.

media.credit: Benreis · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Benreis

questions.description: A cake that looks like a stone floor, but luckily doesn't taste like one.
questions.question: It's a butter cake, often baked in a Gugelhupf pan, with light and dark swirls inside. Why is part of the batter dark?
hints: The cake is named after a kind of stone.
The ingredient comes from beans that grow in the tropics.
The dark part tastes of chocolate.

media.author: Ji-Elle

questions.description: A number that sounds more like a house number than a baking ingredient.
questions.question: In German kitchens, this flour is Type 405. Which grain is it milled from?
hints: It's the most common grain for cakes and bread rolls.
It grows golden yellow in the fields, with short ears.
Most pasta is made from it too.
questions.fun_fact: The number 405 means that 100 grams (3.5 oz) of the flour contain about 405 milligrams of minerals.

media.author: Veganbaking.net from USA

questions.question: You cut into a thick Stollen full of raisins and powdered sugar. When in the year is it mainly eaten?
hints: It is usually cold outside then.
Many houses are decorated with string lights then.
Santa Claus is busy then.
questions.fun_fact: The Dresdner Christstollen is famous: Dresden even holds a Stollen festival every year with a giant Stollen.

media.author: Cornischong at lb.wikipedia

questions.answer: So they don't stick to the baking sheet
hints: You simply eat the wafer along with the macaroon.
Macaroon dough is very sticky.
Without it, the macaroons are hard to get off the baking sheet.
questions.fun_fact: Oblaten are made of nothing but flour and water, baked wafer-thin.

media.author: Stacy Spensley

questions.description: The sheet-pan classic without which Grandma's coffee table would be only half as nice.
questions.question: What topping is on this sheet cake?
hints: It is made from flour, sugar and butter.
You rub it between your fingers into little crumbs.
You also find this topping on a sweet pastry swirl at the bakery.
questions.fun_fact: Streuselkuchen is considered a specialty from Silesia and was often baked for family celebrations.

media.author: Anja Osenberg

A popular pastry swirl at the bakery is filled with them too.
questions.fun_fact: A single poppy seed head can hold more than a thousand tiny seeds.

media.author: Maksym Kozlenko

hints: It is very light and fluffy.
It is made in a spinning machine.
Its name sounds like the soft fluffy stuff people use to take off makeup.
questions.fun_fact: The cotton candy machine was co-invented in 1897 by a dentist.

media.author: Dietmar Rabich

questions.description: An appliance that promises love the moment you open it.

hints: The batter is runny and gets poured in.
What comes out has a grid pattern.
At fairs you often get them heart-shaped with powdered sugar.
questions.fun_fact: Heart-shaped waffles are especially popular in Germany and Scandinavia.

media.author: Donovan Govan.

questions.question: Yellow is to lemon drop as black is to …?
hints: It's a kind of candy.
It comes as wheels or sticks.
Some people love it, others find it gross, especially the salty kind.
questions.fun_fact: Licorice is made from the root of the licorice plant.

media.author: Matthew Paul  Argall

hints: It's a lot like the wafer handed out in church.
This ingredient is also found in potatoes.
It's also used to thicken sauces.
questions.fun_fact: Nuremberg's Elisenlebkuchen are traditionally baked on Oblaten (thin wafers) so the dough doesn't stick to the baking sheet.

media.author: Maja Dumat from Deutschland (Germany)

hints: It is white.
It comes from a farm animal.
You also pour it over cereal.
questions.fun_fact: The company Dr. Oetker from Bielefeld has been selling pudding mix for more than 100 years.

In other regions, the same fair is called “Kirmes”.

You dance in a meadow of lilies of the valley

The next day is a public holiday in Germany.
At midnight, the month changes.
questions.fun_fact: Many villages put up a decorated maypole for May 1, often with a big party around it.

media.author: Bernhard Nowotny, bnow@gmx.de

Three of the four German words start with the same letter.

Ash Wednesday comes soon after.

media.author: Raimond Spekking

The walls are curved so you look tall or wide.

media.author: Gaius Cornelius

The show happens in a big round tent with a ring in the middle.

media.author: Marc-Lautenbacher

You write and draw on it.

media.author: Buchling at de.wikipedia

media.author: Robert Cudmore

media.author: Dietmar Rabich

media.author: DoceanparkHK

Hundreds of thousands sought safety in Germany in 2015.

questions.fun_fact: Around 1980, even boxing legend Muhammad Ali advertised Capri-Sonne.

media.credit: Cbliu · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Cbliu

questions.description: For a long time, ringing the doorbell was its best sales pitch.
questions.question: It comes from Vorwerk in Wuppertal, has been made since 1930 and is often sold door to door. What is the “Kobold” for?
hints: It has a motor and is pretty loud.
You use it mostly on carpets.
Crumbs and dust disappear inside it.
questions.fun_fact: Vorwerk also sells the Thermomix, which weighs, stirs and cooks.

media.credit: guillanst · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: guillanst

questions.description: Smaller than a ruler, but found in almost every jacket pocket.
questions.question: It comes from Hamburg, sits in a small twist-up tube and was invented in 1909. What do you use a Labello for?
hints: You need it especially often in winter.
You put it on your face.
It makes your mouth soft and smooth.
questions.fun_fact: The name Labello comes from the Latin words “labium” (lip) and “bellus” (beautiful).

media.credit: Dietmar Rabich · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Dietmar Rabich

questions.description: He had so much money that even emperors ran a tab with him.
questions.question: Which merchant from Augsburg was nicknamed “the Rich” and lent huge sums to emperors?
hints: He lived around the year 1500.
He made a lot of money from silver and copper.
A social housing estate in Augsburg is still named after his family today.
questions.fun_fact: In the Fuggerei in Augsburg, an apartment still costs only 0.88 euros a year in rent, not counting utilities.

media.credit: Diego Delso · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Diego Delso

questions.description: A game so beautiful that computers fell to their knees in front of it.
questions.question: “But can it run Crysis?” became an internet joke about the game by Frankfurt company Crytek. When did Crysis come out?
hints: Crytek had already released “Far Cry” in 2004.
The first iPhone came out the same year.
The soccer World Cup in Germany had been just one year earlier.
questions.fun_fact: Crytek was founded in Coburg in 1999 by the brothers Cevat, Avni and Faruk Yerli.

media.credit: PantheraLeo1359531 · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: PantheraLeo1359531

questions.description: Open-air theater with a horse on stage and cold feet in the audience.
questions.question: In the St. Martin's play, the actor playing St. Martin draws his sword. What for?
questions.answer: To cut his cloak in half
wrong_answers: To light the St. Martin's bonfire
To catch the St. Martin's goose
hints: He uses it to do something kind for someone.
Back then, Martin was a Roman soldier on horseback.
In front of him, a freezing beggar sits at the city gate of Amiens.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says that the following night Jesus appeared to Martin in a dream, wearing his half of the cloak.

media.credit: Triplec85 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Triplec85

questions.description: A game where you bang a wooden spoon on the floor and nobody tells you off.
questions.question: In the party game Topfschlagen, you find the pot while blindfolded. What do you get then?
hints: It's a game played at children's birthday parties.
It's a small reward for whoever finds the pot.
It usually tastes sweet.
questions.fun_fact: When the other children shout “Hot!”, you're very close to the pot; when they shout “Cold!”, you're far away.

media.credit: Abinayasekar357 · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Abinayasekar357

questions.description: A Sunday that turns up looking rather bushy in Bavaria.
questions.question: What is the Sunday before Easter called, when many churches bless bundles of boxwood and pussy willow?
hints: It marks the day Jesus rode into Jerusalem.
Back then, people laid branches on the road in front of him.
Those branches came from trees that grow in warm, southern lands.
questions.fun_fact: People often tuck the blessed bundles behind the cross in the living room, where they stay all year.

media.credit: DALIBRI · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: DALIBRI

questions.description: A date when grown-ups are officially allowed to be silly.
questions.question: Fill in the blank: On November 11 at 11:11 a.m., the Rhineland kicks off the …
hints: In Cologne and Düsseldorf, lots of people then party in costume in the streets.
It lasts until Ash Wednesday.
There are already spring, summer, fall and winter.
questions.fun_fact: Eleven is seen as the fools' number; some read it as “E-L-F” for “Egalité, Liberté, Fraternité”.

media.credit: Raimond Spekking · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Raimond Spekking

questions.description: A celebration with so many candles that the fire department gets nervous.
questions.question: I'm a Catholic celebration for children around nine, often on Weißer Sonntag (the Sunday after Easter), with a candle and the host. What am I?
hints: The children are usually in third grade.
Girls often wear a white dress, boys a suit.
The children receive the host for the very first time.
questions.fun_fact: Weißer Sonntag (“White Sunday”) got its name because the newly baptized once wore their white baptism robes for the last time on that day.

media.credit: Dietmar Rabich · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Dietmar Rabich

questions.description: Pumpkins and lanterns, fighting over who gets the best fall evenings.
questions.question: You go door to door for Halloween on October 31. How many days later is St. Martin's Day?
hints: St. Martin's Day is in November.
Its date is written with the same number twice.
In Germany, St. Martin's Day falls on the same day the carnival season begins.
questions.fun_fact: In Germany, October 31 is also Reformation Day, a public holiday in several states.

media.credit: F0i · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: F0i

questions.description: A wooden toy whose racket the neighbors, for once, don't complain about.
questions.question: During Holy Week, the church bells fall silent. Why do children in some villages walk the streets with wooden rattles then?
questions.answer: They stand in for the bells
hints: They usually go out at set times of day.
The custom usually ends on Holy Saturday, just before Easter.
Normally, something high up in the church tower does this job.
questions.fun_fact: Children are told that the bells fly to Rome over Easter.

media.credit: Dguendel · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Dguendel

questions.description: A saint whose worst enemies turned out to be poultry.
questions.question: I didn't want to become a bishop, so I hid in a barn, but cackling geese gave me away. Who am I?
hints: Before that, I was a Roman soldier.
In November, children walk through the streets with lanterns for me.
My day is November 11.
questions.fun_fact: That's why many families in Germany put a roast “Martinsgans” (Martin's goose) on the table in November.

media.credit: Les Hull · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Les Hull

questions.description: A bunny that would rather hide things than eat them.
questions.question: The Easter Bunny has hidden colorful eggs in the yard. What do the children do next?
hints: The eggs are in the grass and behind bushes.
Many children bring a little basket for it.
Whoever finds the most is the happiest.
questions.fun_fact: The Easter Bunny was first mentioned in writing in 1682, by a doctor from Heidelberg.

media.credit: Kerbla Edzerdla · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Kerbla Edzerdla

questions.description: A day off in spring when lots of people still get up early to march through town with flags.
questions.question: May 1 is a day off in Germany, and labor unions march through the cities with flags. What do they traditionally demonstrate for?
hints: The tradition goes back to the 19th century.
It started with protests in an American city in 1886.
In German, the holiday is also called “Tag der Arbeit” (Labor Day).
questions.fun_fact: May 1 is a public holiday in many countries all over the world.

media.credit: Nick Catalano from Chicago, United States of America · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Nick Catalano from Chicago, United States of America

questions.description: Craft time with glue, tissue paper and lots of excitement.
questions.question: In the fall, children in German kindergartens make lanterns. What for?
hints: People sing songs together during it.
You walk through the streets with them in the dark.
At the front there's often a man in a red cloak riding a horse.
questions.fun_fact: Lanterns used to hold real candles; today they mostly have small electric light sticks.

media.credit: MIKI Yoshihito. (#mikiyoshihito) · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: MIKI Yoshihito. (#mikiyoshihito)

questions.description: A cone that's almost as tall as the child carrying it.
questions.question: You arrive for your first day of school with your Schultüte. What is traditionally inside it?
hints: The cone is a gift from parents or grandparents.
Often you may only open it after the first lesson.
Chocolate and gummy bears are popular.
questions.fun_fact: The Schultüte has been around for over 200 years, and children were once told that it grew on a Schultüte tree.

media.credit: Michael Coghlan from Adelaide, Australia · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Michael Coghlan from Adelaide, Australia

questions.description: Finally, a photo where nobody can complain about their hair.
questions.question: In Würzburg, Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen discovered rays that let doctors look inside the body. When was that?
hints: The first cars were already on the road.
There was no television yet.
It won him the very first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901.
questions.fun_fact: One of the first X-ray images shows the hand of his wife, Anna Bertha, wedding ring and all.

media.credit: Nevit Dilmen (talk) · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Nevit Dilmen (talk)

questions.description: Two plus two is four, and anyone who disagrees gets in trouble with a certain Adam.
questions.question: When Germans say “nach Adam Riese” (“according to Adam Riese”), they mean a real master of arithmetic. In which century did he live?
hints: He wrote arithmetic books in German instead of Latin.
He lived at the same time as Martin Luther.
He was born around the time Columbus reached America.
questions.fun_fact: His books taught many people to calculate with Arabic numerals instead of Roman numerals.

media.credit: Jacobolus · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jacobolus

questions.description: Some words secretly belong to a company, and nobody notices.
questions.question: Many Germans say “Tesa” instead of “Klebefilm” (sticky tape): a brand became an everyday word. Which of these words is NOT a brand name?
hints: The word existed long before any of these companies.
You need one when you've scraped your knee.
A well-known brand of it is Hansaplast.
questions.fun_fact: The name tesa comes from Beiersdorf employee Elsa Tesmer: TEsmer and elSA.

media.credit: BarberJP · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: BarberJP

questions.description: One hole next to another, and still a huge idea.
questions.question: In 1884, Paul Nipkow, then a student in Berlin, patented a spinning disk with holes arranged in a spiral. What was it for?
hints: The holes scan something line by line.
The patent was called “Electric Telescope.”
The device it led to is in almost every living room today.
questions.fun_fact: Nipkow himself never built a working device with his disk.

media.credit: Unknown authorUnknown author or not provided · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Unknown authorUnknown author or not provided

questions.description: Anyone who says dreams mean nothing never met this chemist.
questions.question: I was a chemist, and half-asleep I supposedly saw a snake biting its own tail. That's how I came up with the benzene ring. Who am I?
hints: I taught for many years at the University of Bonn.
Benzene is made of six carbon atoms, which I arranged in a ring.
My surname sounds French and ends with an accent.
questions.fun_fact: He only told the story of his dream in 1890, at a party for the 25th birthday of his benzene formula.

media.credit: Tzim78 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Tzim78

questions.description: A housemate who never pays rent but throws a party in the hallway every night.
questions.question: In the well-known German children's song, which figure dances “in unserm Haus herum, dideldum”?
hints: The song is a very old circle game for small children.
Long ago this figure was a bogeyman used to scare children.
In the song, his name comes after a “Bi-Ba-”.
questions.fun_fact: The Butzemann is a close relative of the “Buhmann”; both were figures used to scare children in the old days.

media.credit: Zoltan Kluger · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Zoltan Kluger

questions.description: This animal stands at attention like a guard, only much fluffier.
questions.question: In German, this animal has the same name as the little earth spirits that live underground in old legends. What is it?
hints: It lives in big groups in southern Africa.
One of the group always keeps watch while the others eat.
Its German name means “little earth man”.
questions.fun_fact: Meerkats belong to the mongoose family and can even eat venomous scorpions.

media.credit: Giles Laurent · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Giles Laurent

questions.description: A forest spirit that sounds more fragile than it is.
questions.question: A good forest spirit, seen only by children born on a Sunday, grants Peter Munk three wishes. Where does the Glasmännlein live?
hints: The story comes from Wilhelm Hauff’s fairy tale “Das kalte Herz” (“The Cold Heart”).
His evil rival is the Holländer-Michel, a giant raftsman.
The region is famous for cuckoo clocks and a cherry cake.
questions.fun_fact: In the tale, you call the Glasmännlein with a verse that begins “Schatzhauser im grünen Tannenwald” (“Treasure-keeper in the green fir forest”).

media.credit: AlejandroLinaresGarcia · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: AlejandroLinaresGarcia

questions.description: The longest nap in German history, and no alarm clock in sight.
questions.question: I sleep inside the Kyffhäuser, and my beard grows through a stone table. When ravens stop circling the mountain, I'll wake up. Who am I?
hints: I was an emperor from the Hohenstaufen family.
I lived in the 12th century and went on a crusade.
My nickname means “red beard” in Italian.
questions.fun_fact: At the Kyffhäuser Monument, a stone figure of Barbarossa waking up sits below the statue of Emperor Wilhelm I on horseback.

media.credit: Frank Schulenburg · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Frank Schulenburg

questions.description: A present from someone you don't know, and this one time it's allowed.
questions.question: When do school classes and offices most like to do “Wichteln”?
hints: In Wichteln, you secretly draw a name and give that person a present.
It's also the time when people bake Plätzchen.
Christmas Eve comes soon after.
questions.fun_fact: In Scandinavia, a gnome called “Tomte” or “Nisse” brings the presents at Christmas.

media.credit: Isiwal · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Isiwal

questions.description: A tenant who hasn't moved out in centuries and still wants no trouble with the landlord.
questions.question: He rattles his rusty chain and annoys King Julius the 111th. Where does the ghost Hui Buh haunt?
hints: Hui Buh calls himself the only officially licensed castle ghost.
The castle's name starts with the German word for a knight's fortress.
It ends with the German word for a corner or edge.
questions.fun_fact: In the old audio plays, Hans Clarin was the voice of Hui Buh; in the 2006 movie he was played by Michael “Bully” Herbig.

media.credit: Aconcagua (talk) · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Aconcagua (talk)

questions.description: When socks and keys vanish at night, people like to blame a creature from the old legends.
questions.question: Which of these figures is NOT a kobold?
hints: Three of the four are small spirits of the house or of ships.
The one you're looking for isn't small at all.
He is a big, bearded mountain spirit who plays tricks on travelers.
questions.fun_fact: The Klabautermann is a ship's kobold: sailors believed he warned them of danger on board.

media.credit: Richard Brakenburgh · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Richard Brakenburgh

questions.description: A building project with very unusual competition from down below.
questions.question: Legend says this cathedral’s builder made a bet with the devil, who built a water channel to this city. From which city did it start?
hints: The city was already a major city in Roman times.
It was once home to Roman emperors and is seen as one of Germany’s oldest cities.
The Porta Nigra stands there.
questions.fun_fact: The real Roman aqueduct carried water from the Eifel hills to Cologne, about 95 km (59 miles) away.

media.credit: Thomas Wolf, www.foto-tw.de · CC BY-SA 3.0 de · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Thomas Wolf, www.foto-tw.de

questions.description: A trip where you pack a napkin instead of a suitcase.
questions.question: This painting shows a legendary land where roast pigeons fly straight into your mouth. What is it called?
hints: There, the laziest person counts as the best.
To get in, you first have to eat your way through a mountain of semolina pudding.
Its name comes from an old German word for a lazy idler.
questions.fun_fact: Pieter Bruegel the Elder painted his famous picture of this land in 1567.

media.credit: Pieter Brueghel the Elder · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Pieter Brueghel the Elder

questions.description: The only place where shouting out is actually encouraged.
questions.question: In the Kasperle puppet show, the crocodile sneaks up. Kasperle can't see it, but the children can. What do they shout?
hints: The children in the audience see more than Kasperle does.
The crocodile is up to no good.
He should be careful.
questions.fun_fact: Kasperle carries a wooden slapstick, and he usually uses it to chase off the robber or the crocodile in the end.

media.credit: Alf van Beem · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Alf van Beem

questions.description: Too young for the big party, even at over a hundred.
questions.question: I'm only 127 years old, my raven Abraxas can talk, and I'm not allowed on the Blocksberg yet. Who am I?
hints: Otfried Preußler made me up.
I want to be a good witch, which makes the other witches very angry.
My name says that I'm not big.
questions.fun_fact: Otfried Preußler's “Die kleine Hexe” (The Little Witch) came out in 1957 and has been translated into more than 40 languages.

media.credit: Pearson Scott Foresman · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Pearson Scott Foresman

questions.description: A neighbor who never comes over for coffee because he'd ruin the rug.
questions.question: I live deep down in the mill pond, I have green hair, and the hem of my coat is always dripping. Who am I?
hints: I can stay underwater much longer than any human.
Otfried Preußler wrote a book about my little son.
In German, my name is also a zodiac sign: Aquarius.
questions.fun_fact: In many legends, you can spot a Wassermann in disguise because the hem of his coat is always wet.

media.credit: M J Roscoe · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: M J Roscoe

questions.description: A valley older than any river that splashes around in it today.
questions.question: Northern Germany is crossed by wide ancient valleys called Urstromtäler, such as the Berlin one. What created them?
hints: The valleys formed a few tens of thousands of years ago.
Back then, Scandinavia lay under a huge sheet of ice.
When the ice thawed, the water flowed off in giant streams toward the North Sea.
questions.fun_fact: The Spree flows through Berlin in a valley once dug by a much bigger stream of meltwater.

media.credit: Newt713 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Newt713

questions.description: A little stone with a very, very long journey behind it.
questions.question: I'm a huge stone in a field in northern Germany, but I come from Scandinavia. Glaciers brought me here. What am I?
hints: I came to Germany during the Ice Age.
Sometimes I weigh several hundred tons.
My name comes from a Latin word meaning “to wander.”
questions.fun_fact: Many old village churches in northern Germany were built from split erratic boulders.

media.credit: Mat Fascione · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Mat Fascione

questions.description: A place where the trees have more say than the people.
questions.question: Germany's first national park opened here in 1970. It borders the Czech Republic, and its highest peak is the Großer Arber. Which mountain range is it?
hints: This range is in southeastern Germany.
On the Czech side, it continues as the Bohemian Forest.
It lies in Lower Bavaria and the Upper Palatinate.
questions.fun_fact: In the national park, dead trees aren't cleared away; the forest is allowed to turn back into wilderness.

media.credit: Matthias · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Matthias

questions.description: When the North Sea drops by for a visit, you need a good hill.
questions.question: On the Halligen, houses stand on mounds like these so they stay dry during “Land unter” (when storm tides flood the islands). What is such a mound called?
hints: People built the mound by piling up earth.
Often several farms stand together on one mound.
In some regions the word is also said as “Wurt”.
questions.fun_fact: During “Land unter”, the houses of a Hallig stick out of the North Sea like tiny islands.

media.credit: Michael Gäbler · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Michael Gäbler

questions.description: A mountain with a double life: a hiking spot by day, a party zone in legend.
questions.question: In the legend of the minnesinger Tannhäuser, the Hörselberg near Eisenach has a second name. What is it?
hints: Richard Wagner turned the legend into an opera.
Tannhäuser is said to have spent a whole year under a spell inside the mountain, then asked the Pope for forgiveness.
Inside the mountain lived a goddess of love who also gave her name to a planet.
questions.fun_fact: Wagner's opera “Tannhäuser” is also set at Wartburg Castle, which lies very close to the Hörselberg.

media.credit: Metilsteiner · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Metilsteiner

questions.description: When she shakes out her pillows, all of Germany turns white.
questions.question: In the fairy tale “Frau Holle” (Mother Holle), the girl jumps after her lost spindle and lands with Frau Holle. What does she jump into?
hints: She had been sitting at this spot to spin.
The spot was outside by the road near the house.
In the old days, people pulled water up from it with a bucket.
questions.fun_fact: The Hoher Meißner in Hesse is said to be Frau Holle's home, and it even has a Frau Holle pond.

media.credit: Peter van der Sluijs · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Peter van der Sluijs

questions.description: An animal with a bad reputation: it can't escape the jokes about how brave it is.
questions.question: In German, a timid person is an “Angsthase” (scaredy hare). How fast can a real brown hare run when it flees?
hints: It is faster than any human who has ever run.
About as fast as a car on a country road.
It's more than 50 but less than 100 km/h.
questions.fun_fact: When they flee, brown hares make lightning-fast zigzag turns to shake off foxes; 70 km/h is about 43 mph.

media.credit: Adam Ward · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Adam Ward

questions.description: A job where you have tens of thousands of coworkers, and every one of them can sting.
questions.question: This person keeps bee colonies, often wears a hat with a veil and harvests honey in summer. What is this person called?
hints: The job has to do with insects.
Their bees live in wooden boxes called hives.
The job's name is the insect's name plus a word for someone who looks after something.
questions.fun_fact: Honeybees use a “waggle dance” to show each other which way to fly to find flowers.

media.credit: Alabama Extension · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Alabama Extension

questions.description: The secret boss behind every glass of milk on the breakfast table.
questions.question: Which cattle breed is the most common dairy cow in Germany?
hints: It first came from northern Germany and the Netherlands.
Around the world it is called Holstein Friesian.
Its coat has black and white patches.
questions.fun_fact: In Germany, one cow of this breed often gives more than 9,000 liters (about 2,400 gallons) of milk a year.

media.credit: David Adam Kess · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: David Adam Kess

questions.description: A city dweller who never pays rent but still grabs every seat in the square.
questions.question: I coo in market squares and peck crumbs off the cobblestones. In a German saying, I sit on the roof. Who am I?
hints: I like to hang out at train stations and on statues.
In the old days, I delivered letters.
With an olive branch in my beak, I'm a symbol of peace.
questions.fun_fact: Homing pigeons can find their way back to their loft from hundreds of kilometers away.

media.credit: AlexanderRahm · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: AlexanderRahm

questions.description: Anyone walking barefoot through the heath had better get this question right.
questions.question: Three of these snakes found in Germany are harmless to humans. Which one isn't?
hints: It likes to live in moors, heaths and the mountains.
It has a dark zigzag band along its back.
It's also the only venomous snake living wild in Britain.
questions.fun_fact: Adders don't lay eggs: they give birth to live young.

media.credit: Chromdioxid · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Chromdioxid

questions.description: An artist who hides its work where nobody will ever look.
questions.question: An animal ate these tunnels under the bark of a spruce tree. Which animal was it?
hints: The animal is only a few millimeters long.
After dry summers, it turned whole spruce forests in the Harz mountains brown.
One well-known species is called “typographus” (the printer) because its tunnels look like writing.
questions.fun_fact: The female lays her eggs along a main tunnel, and each larva then eats its own side tunnel out from there.

media.credit: Tõnu Pani · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Tõnu Pani

questions.description: A fish with a double life: depending on the sea, it goes by a different name.
questions.question: In the Baltic Sea, Germans call this fish “Dorsch”. What German name does it go by in the North Sea and at the fish counter?
hints: It's one of the most important food fish in Europe.
In Norway, it's dried to make stockfish.
Its name starts almost like the English word “cable”.
questions.fun_fact: Its liver is used to make cod liver oil, which many children once had to swallow by the spoonful.

media.credit: Wilhelm Thomas Fiege · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Wilhelm Thomas Fiege

questions.description: It looks like it forgot to say “stop” while growing its legs.
questions.question: A harvestman has eight legs, but it spins no webs and has no venom. Which animal group does it still belong to?
hints: Insects have only six legs.
Scorpions and mites belong to this group too.
The best-known animals in this group build webs.
questions.fun_fact: If an enemy grabs a harvestman by the leg, it drops the leg, which keeps twitching for a while.

media.credit: Bernard DUPONT from FRANCE · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bernard DUPONT from FRANCE

questions.description: A concert from the bird world where you never get to see the singer.
questions.question: Listen: which bird makes this sound?
hints: It builds huge nests on church towers and chimneys.
Instead of singing, it clatters its beak together.
Legend says it brings the babies.
questions.fun_fact: White storks are almost silent, so they talk to each other by clattering their beaks; that's why Germans call them “Klapperstorch” (clatter stork).

media.credit: felix.blume · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: felix.blume

background.credit: Hanlu Cao · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
background.author: Hanlu Cao

questions.description: A prank that makes everyone check under the covers before bedtime.
questions.question: Max and Moritz put beetles like these in Uncle Fritz's bed. Who wrote the story?
hints: The author also drew the pictures for his stories himself.
He is seen as one of the forefathers of the comic strip.
He also wrote “Die fromme Helene”.
questions.fun_fact: Before they can fly, cockchafers spend three to four years underground as grubs.

media.credit: Frank.Vassen · CC BY 2.0 · Flickr via Openverse
media.author: Frank.Vassen

questions.description: A lumberjack with no saw, but with a very impressive set of teeth.
questions.question: The animal that gnawed this tree like this was almost wiped out in Germany. Which animal group does it belong to?
hints: It builds dams and lodges by the water.
Its tail is wide and flat like a trowel.
Mice and squirrels belong to this group too.
questions.fun_fact: Around 1900, only about 200 beavers were left along the Elbe; today Germany has tens of thousands again.

media.credit: NPS Staff · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: NPS Staff

questions.description: A fox and a devil in a single word: German never takes a break.
questions.question: In German, “hundemüde” (dog-tired) means very tired. What does “fuchsteufelswild” mean?
hints: The word describes a mood.
Rumpelstiltskin is exactly like this at the end of his fairy tale.
Someone like this stamps their foot and shouts.
questions.fun_fact: Other German words use animals to say “very”, too: “bärenstark” (bear-strong), “mausetot” (mouse-dead) or “aalglatt” (eel-smooth).

media.credit: The Forest Vixen's CC Photo Stream · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: The Forest Vixen's CC Photo Stream

questions.description: A sea creature that just lies there at low tide and waits for the water to come back.
questions.question: It is blue-black, holds on to stones in the Wadden Sea with strong threads and often ends up in the cooking pot. What is it?
hints: It lives by the thousands in large beds on the mudflats.
It is often cooked in white wine with vegetables.
Its name sounds just like what you use to lift heavy things.
questions.fun_fact: Its sticky threads are called byssus, and scientists study them to make glues that hold under water.

media.credit: Olgierd Rudak · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Olgierd Rudak

questions.description: It looks like Grandma's tabby, but it will definitely not let you pet it.
questions.question: This shy cat with a bushy, black-ringed tail lives in German forests like the Hainich. Which animal is it?
hints: It's not a runaway pet, but it looks very much like a striped house cat.
Its tail ends bluntly in a black tip, and it has no ear tufts.
Its name says it's the opposite of a tame cat.
questions.fun_fact: In Thuringia, the village of Hütscheroda has a whole “Wildkatzendorf” (wildcat village), where you can watch these shy animals.

media.credit: Lviatour · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Lviatour

questions.description: Outside, it looks like someone has wrapped the whole world in cotton balls.
questions.question: You wake up on a fall morning and the fog is so thick you can hardly see the street. When does fog like this usually clear?
hints: Fog forms when damp air cools down a lot.
When the air warms up again, it goes away.
As the sun climbs higher and warms the air, it disappears.
questions.fun_fact: Fog is really a cloud lying right on the ground.

media.credit: John Sutton · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: John Sutton

questions.description: People who just fell in love don't need an elevator. They float up all by themselves.
questions.question: In the German saying, someone newly and blissfully in love floats on “Wolke …” what number?
hints: Many fairy tales treat this number as magic.
Snow White lives with this many dwarfs.
A week has this many days.
questions.fun_fact: In English, people in love don't float on cloud seven. They float on “cloud nine.”

media.credit: Novoklimov · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Novoklimov

questions.description: By now your hair doesn't matter anymore, and your umbrella is gone too.
questions.question: The weather report warns of a hurricane-force wind on the North Sea coast. What number does it have on the Beaufort scale?
hints: The scale starts at 0, which means no wind at all.
Level 9 is called a strong gale, and it goes higher still.
Hurricane force is at the very top of the scale, the same number as the months in a year.
questions.fun_fact: Irish-born British naval officer Francis Beaufort came up with the scale around 1805 for sailing ships; back then it described how many sails a ship could carry.

media.credit: Bernd Thaller from Graz, Austria · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bernd Thaller from Graz, Austria

questions.description: A balloon with a science degree: it collects data until it pops.
questions.question: Germany's weather service, the Deutscher Wetterdienst, sends up weather balloons every day that only burst at about 30 km (19 miles). In which layer of the air does that happen?
hints: The weather itself happens lower down; the balloon flies above it.
The ozone layer is also in this layer.
It is the second layer from the bottom.
questions.fun_fact: Because the air up there is so thin, the balloon swells to many times its starting size as it rises.

media.credit: Photouploadforscience · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Photouploadforscience

questions.description: Germans check the weather app more often than the fridge, and that's saying something.
questions.question: Before a thunderstorm, the wind often drops and the air feels heavy. What does the German saying “die Ruhe vor dem Sturm” mean?
questions.answer: A deceptive quiet before something exciting happens
wrong_answers: A break after everything is over
A place that never gets storms
hints: The saying fits well before a big exam or a big game.
In movies, it's often said just before the big showdown.
Right after it, things really get going.
questions.fun_fact: Before thunderstorms, the wind really does often go still for a moment before cold gusts burst out of the storm cloud.

media.credit: Pattaya Patrol from Pattaya · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Pattaya Patrol from Pattaya

questions.description: A paint box that pops open in the sky for a moment after every rain shower.
questions.question: Which color does NOT appear in a rainbow?
hints: A rainbow is made from sunlight.
The rainbow's colors are the colors sunlight splits into, and this one isn't among them.
It's the color of the night.
questions.fun_fact: In a double rainbow, the colors in the outer arc appear in exactly the reverse order.

media.credit: ruth e · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: ruth e

questions.description: The sky is wearing lipstick, and that's bad news for your picnic.
questions.question: I paint the sky red and orange just before the sun comes up. An old weather saying claims bad weather often follows me. What am I?
hints: You mostly see me if you get up very early.
My partner in the evening promises good weather instead.
Sailors have an old rhyme: when they see me, they take warning.
questions.fun_fact: The saying is often right: a red sky in the morning frequently means clouds from a low-pressure system are coming in from the west.

media.credit: Eirian Evans · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Eirian Evans

questions.description: Winter mornings: when even your blanket files a request for an extension.
questions.question: In winter, rain falls and freezes at once on the cold road. What forms?
hints: Afterwards, people walking and cars slip easily.
It lies on the ground as a thin, see-through layer.
It is ice that is extra slippery.
questions.fun_fact: In German, leading someone “aufs Glatteis” (onto the black ice) means trying to trick them with a tricky question.

media.credit: CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

questions.description: Finally, a walk where the squirrels have to look up to you.
questions.question: You walk on wooden boardwalks high up among the branches, with no harness, even with a stroller. In the Bavarian Forest, it ends at an egg-shaped tower. What is it?
hints: You don't need any climbing gear.
You're at eye level with woodpeckers and the tops of the trees.
The name says you walk along the very tops of the trees.
questions.fun_fact: The treetop walkway in Bavarian Forest National Park near Neuschönau is about 1,300 m (4,300 ft) long and was one of the first in Germany.

media.credit: Siarhei Besarab · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Siarhei Besarab

questions.description: “Laterne, Laterne, Sonne, Mond und Sterne” – and a cloak that is suddenly only half as big.
questions.question: This is a lantern procession on November 11. According to legend, who did the saint remembered that day share his cloak with?
hints: The saint was a soldier and rode a horse.
It was a cold winter day, and the man by the roadside was freezing.
The man was very poor and asked for help.
questions.fun_fact: The Martinsgans (St. Martin's goose) supposedly comes from a legend: Martin hid in a goose pen to avoid being made a bishop, but the cackling geese gave him away.

media.credit: Helge Klaus Rieder · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Helge Klaus Rieder

questions.description: Snacking with guaranteed scratches: these vines make you pay with scrapes on your arms.
questions.question: In summer, hard red Brombeeren still hang at the edge of the forest. What color are they when they're ripe and sweet?
hints: Brombeeren ripen in late summer, around August.
Ripe ones are soft and come off the stem easily.
They are as dark as the night.
questions.fun_fact: A blackberry isn't really a berry at all, but a cluster of many tiny fruits, each with its own little seed.

media.credit: Eugen Reichenbach · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Eugen Reichenbach

questions.description: Purple, round, and at Grandma's Sunday lunch rarely far from the dumpling.
questions.question: In Germany, this vegetable is often served with the Sunday roast. Which group of vegetables does it belong to?
hints: It grows above the ground as a thick, firm head.
It belongs to the same plant family as mustard and rapeseed.
Sauerkraut is made from its pale brother.
questions.fun_fact: Whether it's called Rotkohl or Blaukraut depends on the region, and in fact vinegar makes it redder and baking soda makes it bluer.

media.credit: Elrond · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Elrond

questions.description: When clouds turn sour, for once it isn’t the neighbor’s fault.
questions.question: In the 1980s, Germans feared “Waldsterben” (forest dieback) from acid rain. Which gas from coal power plants mainly made the rain acidic?
hints: It has a sharp smell, like a match that has just burned out.
Volcanoes also release huge amounts of it when they erupt.
Its chemical formula is SO₂.
questions.fun_fact: Thanks to filters in power plants, Germany’s sulfur emissions have dropped by more than 90 percent since 1990.

media.credit: Mozzihh · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Mozzihh

questions.description: Bite into these and you'll pull a face like Grandpa reading the electricity bill.
questions.question: These sour berries hang like little strings of pearls in bunches and come in red, white or black. Which berry is it?
hints: It grows on a bush in the garden.
People often strip them off the stems with a fork.
Its German name comes from a saint's day at the end of June.
questions.fun_fact: Blackcurrants contain about three times as much vitamin C as lemons.

media.credit: Coen · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Coen

questions.description: Tall, yellow and always a little too cheerful.
questions.question: Sunflowers grow taller than grown-ups, and in the fall their heads are full of seeds. Which animals love to eat the seeds?
hints: You can often watch these animals in the garden.
In winter, many people hang these seeds outside for them.
Finches and sparrows are among them.
questions.fun_fact: Young sunflowers turn their heads with the sun during the day, from east to west.

media.credit: Emilrex · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Emilrex

questions.description: Mushroom hunters won't tell even their own family where they found this one.
questions.question: This edible mushroom has a brown cap, a thick, pale stem and a sponge instead of gills under its cap. What is it called?
hints: It counts as one of the finest mushrooms in German forests.
In Italy it's called “porcino.”
Its German name starts with the word for “stone.”
questions.fun_fact: King boletes live in partnership with trees like spruces, beeches and oaks, so they are almost impossible to farm.

media.credit: Simson Petrol simson_petrol · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Simson Petrol simson_petrol

questions.description: Here a vegetable gets buried before it's even properly born.
questions.question: On German asparagus fields you see long ridges of soil like these. Why are they piled up?
wrong_answers: To keep hares away from it
hints: It's about the color of the spears.
It's dark under the ground.
Sunlight would turn the tips green or purple.
questions.fun_fact: By tradition, asparagus is only cut until June 24, St. John's Day (Johannistag), so the plant can recover afterwards.

media.credit: Ahoerstemeier · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ahoerstemeier

questions.description: This is where trees turn into something that fits much better on a shelf.
questions.question: Trucks bring felled spruce logs here, boards and beams come out, and wood shavings lie everywhere. Where do the logs go?
hints: It smells of fresh resin there.
Big machines screech there all day long.
The tool doing the work there has steel teeth.
questions.fun_fact: The sawdust is often pressed into wood pellets that people burn for heating.

media.credit: Karl Peet · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Karl Peet

questions.description: A tree that foresters count more often than other people count sheep before falling asleep.
questions.question: The Harz and the Black Forest have huge spruce forests. What kind of tree is a spruce?
hints: It's one of the most common trees in German forests.
Many Christmas trees are spruces.
It grows cones, and its pointy leaves prick you.
questions.fun_fact: Spruce cones hang down and fall off whole, so the cones on the forest floor are almost never true fir cones.

media.credit: Taxiarchos228 · FAL · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Taxiarchos228

questions.description: A nursery for trees, but without the bedtime story.
questions.question: When foresters plant new trees, they often put young saplings in tubes like these. Why?
hints: The danger walks on four legs.
The attackers love to nibble fresh buds.
Bambi would be the bad guy here.
questions.fun_fact: German foresters call the damage done when deer chew off buds and shoots “Verbiss”.

media.credit: Rept0n1x · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Rept0n1x

questions.description: Two brothers, one father, a forest full of bandits: German family drama at its finest.
questions.question: Who wrote the play “The Robbers”, whose 1782 premiere in Mannheim sent the audience into a frenzy?
hints: At the time, the author was in his early twenties and an army doctor in Stuttgart.
Because he secretly traveled to the performance, he was put under arrest for two weeks.
He later also wrote “William Tell”.
questions.fun_fact: One eyewitness reported that at the premiere, total strangers fell sobbing into each other’s arms.

media.credit: Nemracc · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Nemracc

questions.description: Other kids were still learning to tie their shoes while this boy was practicing piano for the concert hall.
questions.question: I was a child prodigy from Hamburg, brought Bach's St. Matthew Passion back to the stage in 1829 and wrote a famous wedding march. Who am I?
hints: In 1843 I founded Germany's first conservatory, in Leipzig.
My sister Fanny was a gifted composer too.
My grandfather was a famous Jewish philosopher of the Enlightenment and a friend of Lessing.
questions.fun_fact: Mendelssohn was only 20 when he performed the St. Matthew Passion in Berlin, about 100 years after it was written.

media.credit: Jorge Royan · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jorge Royan

questions.description: A place where people used to come home from work with black fingernails.
questions.question: Deep mines full of hard coal, Krupp steel, and miners who call each other “Kumpel”: which region is this?
hints: The region is one of the largest urban areas in Europe.
Bochum, Essen and Gelsenkirchen are part of it.
It is named after a river that flows into the Rhine at Duisburg.
questions.fun_fact: At the end of 2018, the Prosper-Haniel mine in Bottrop closed, ending hard coal mining in the Ruhr area.

media.credit: Adrian Tync · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Adrian Tync

questions.description: A student party with torches, speeches and surprisingly little beer pong.
questions.question: In 1817, fraternity students held a big festival for 300 years of the Reformation and the anniversary of the Battle of Leipzig. Where?
hints: The place is a castle in Thuringia.
Saint Elizabeth is said to have lived there long ago.
Hiding there as “Junker Jörg”, Luther translated the New Testament.
questions.fun_fact: About 500 students came, and many already wore the black, red and gold colors of the Jena fraternity.

media.credit: Waschl87 (Diskussion) · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Waschl87 (Diskussion)

questions.description: A man of words whose name now appears on many street signs.
questions.question: Robert Blum, a leading voice of the democrats in 1848, was born in 1807 to a barrel maker in a city on the Rhine. Which city?
hints: He later lived and worked mostly in Leipzig.
His hometown lies on the left bank of the Rhine.
A Gothic cathedral with two huge towers rises over the city.
questions.fun_fact: In Leipzig, Blum worked as a theater secretary and even helped publish a “General Theater Encyclopedia”.

media.credit: Jörg Braukmann · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jörg Braukmann

questions.description: A student who robbed his teacher of a quiet break.
questions.question: Which mathematician from Braunschweig is said to have added up the numbers 1 to 100 in a flash as a schoolboy?
hints: He was called the “Prince of Mathematicians”.
He appeared on the old 10-Deutsche-Mark bill.
The bell-shaped curve of the normal distribution is named after him.
questions.fun_fact: His trick: 1+100, 2+99, 3+98 … gives 50 times 101, so 5050.

media.credit: Fay, Edward Allen, 1843-1923 · No restrictions · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Fay, Edward Allen, 1843-1923

questions.description: Pitchforks against cannons: that bet didn't end well.
questions.question: In May 1525, a peasant army led by Thomas Müntzer was defeated by the princes in Thuringia. What is this battle called?
hints: A huge panorama painting by Werner Tübke remembers the battle there.
The town lies at the foot of the Kyffhäuser hills.
Today the town is a spa town with “Bad” in its name.
questions.fun_fact: Tübke's Peasants' War Panorama is 123 m (404 ft) long and 14 m (46 ft) high, one of the largest paintings in the world.

media.credit: Rudolf Schiestl · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Rudolf Schiestl

questions.description: A picture book where the parents knew exactly why they were reading it out loud.
questions.question: A doctor from Frankfurt made a children's book with Suppenkaspar, Zappelphilipp and Hans Guck-in-die-Luft. What is it called?
hints: The cover shows a boy with wild, messy hair.
This boy never cuts his fingernails.
His name describes his shaggy hairdo.
questions.fun_fact: Heinrich Hoffmann first drew the book as a Christmas present for his three-year-old son.

media.credit: Thomas Wolf (Der Wolf im Wald) · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Thomas Wolf (Der Wolf im Wald)

questions.description: A poem that has crossed more borders than any tour bus.
questions.question: Schiller wrote it in 1785, Beethoven set it in his 9th Symphony, and today its tune is Europe's anthem. Which poem?
hints: It contains the line “Alle Menschen werden Brüder” (all people become brothers).
A large choir sings it in the symphony's last movement.
Its German first line starts with the feeling named in the title: “…, schöner Götterfunken”.
questions.fun_fact: The European anthem is officially played without words, so that no language is favored.

media.credit: MPD01605 · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: MPD01605

questions.description: A dish with more names than a secret agent.
questions.question: The dish in the photo has a different name almost everywhere in Germany. Where is it mainly called “Reibekuchen”?
hints: It's a region in the west of Germany.
There, people love them at the Christmas market with applesauce.
Cologne and Düsseldorf are in this region.
questions.fun_fact: In Bavaria, potato pancakes are called “Reiberdatschi”.

media.credit: Raimond Spekking · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Raimond Spekking

questions.description: The train rattles above you, and lunch is steaming in front of you.
questions.question: Konnopke's Imbiss has stood under the elevated train on Schönhauser Allee for decades. From 1960, it sold currywurst without what?
hints: In East Germany, one ingredient for sausages was in short supply.
The missing thing normally keeps a sausage in shape.
It's the skin that the sausage meat is stuffed into.
questions.fun_fact: Max Konnopke started in 1930 with a vendor's tray, selling sausages from a kettle.

media.credit: Ansgar Koreng · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ansgar Koreng

questions.description: Sounds like a pug that curled up for a nap, but you won't find it at the vet.
questions.question: Which group does the Rollmops NOT belong to?
hints: A Rollmops comes out of a jar.
It swims in vinegar with onions.
Inside is a rolled-up herring.
questions.fun_fact: In Germany, the Rollmops is the classic “hangover breakfast” after a long night.

media.credit: WDnet · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: WDnet

questions.description: Peter had a rough day. A really minced-up one.
questions.question: At a butcher shop in Berlin, you order a roll with “Hackepeter”. What's on it?
hints: It's made from pork.
It's eaten raw, often with onions.
At party buffets, it's often shaped into a “hedgehog”.
questions.fun_fact: In the 1970s, the “Mettigel”, a hedgehog with pretzel sticks as spikes, was the star of many parties.

media.credit: Roy Zuo · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Roy Zuo

questions.description: A cake that looks like someone threw crumbs all over it, on purpose.
questions.question: For Streuselkuchen, the crumbs are rubbed between your fingers: flour, sugar and what else?
hints: It's firm when it comes out of the fridge.
It makes the crumbs rich and crumbly.
You also spread it on bread.
questions.fun_fact: Streuselkuchen has long been a classic, especially in Silesia and eastern Germany.

media.credit: TGar21 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: TGar21

questions.description: This ham has spent more time in smoke than a barbecue champion.
questions.question: Black Forest ham like the one in the photo is cold-smoked. Over which wood, traditionally?
hints: The tree grows everywhere in the ham's home region.
It is a conifer.
At Christmas, there's often one standing in the living room.
questions.fun_fact: Black Forest ham has protected origin status in the EU: it must be made in the Black Forest.

media.credit: Erich Ferdinand from germany · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Erich Ferdinand from germany

questions.description: A winter outing where a vegetable is the whole point of the trip.
questions.question: Where is the winter “Kohlfahrt” NOT an old tradition?
hints: The Kohlfahrt is a custom from one particular part of Germany.
People hike through the cold pulling a Bollerwagen (handcart), then eat Grünkohl (kale).
The place you're looking for is in the south.
questions.fun_fact: Whoever eats the most Grünkohl on a Kohlfahrt is often crowned “Kohlkönig” (kale king).

media.credit: USDAgov · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: USDAgov

questions.description: A dish that calls for a serious knife and an even more serious appetite.
questions.question: Which dish is a cut from a pig's lower leg, has a crispy crust and comes with a dumpling in Bavaria?
hints: It's a beer garden classic.
There's a bone in the middle.
In Bavarian dialect, people call it “Haxn.”
questions.fun_fact: In northern Germany, people prefer to boil the same cut, and then they call it “Eisbein.”

media.credit: Ianp5a · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ianp5a

questions.description: A spit that keeps turning until everyone is full.
questions.question: Döner in bread, like in the photo, probably only dates back to the 1970s. In which German city did it start?
hints: Back then, a great many people from Turkey lived there.
Today the city is known for its many döner shops.
It is the capital.
questions.fun_fact: Kadir Nurman is said to have sold döner in bread at Berlin's Bahnhof Zoo station in 1972.

media.credit: AleGranholm · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: AleGranholm

questions.description: Its name says cake, its taste says pizza, and it's neither.
questions.question: You're putting the toppings on a classic Flammkuchen. What goes on it?
hints: The topping is pale, not red.
Flammkuchen comes from Alsace, where it's topped very simply.
It also gets little cubes of smoked pork belly.
questions.fun_fact: Bakers in Alsace once tested the heat of their ovens with a flatbread that baked right next to the flames.

media.credit: MOs810 · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: MOs810

questions.description: These beans have clearly been hitting the bacon a little too hard.
questions.question: Dicke Bohnen mit Speck is a classic from the Rhineland. What other German name do Dicke Bohnen go by?
hints: They were once used as animal feed, too.
Botanically, the plant belongs to the vetches.
The name starts with the German word for a female pig.
questions.fun_fact: Dicke Bohnen have been grown in Europe for thousands of years, long before green beans arrived from the Americas.

media.credit: Adam Jones, Ph.D. · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Adam Jones, Ph.D.

questions.description: Caffeine by candlelight: the coziest get-together in December.
questions.question: You're invited to an Adventskaffee (coffee and cake in Advent). When is it traditionally held?
hints: Coffee and cake aren't served for breakfast.
The Advent wreath has something to do with the timing.
On this day, a new candle is lit on the Advent wreath.
questions.fun_fact: The first Sunday of Advent always falls between November 27 and December 3.

media.credit: Semipepino · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Semipepino

questions.description: A wreath that gets a little brighter every Sunday.
questions.question: “Advent, Advent, ein Lichtlein brennt” is how a poem about this wreath begins. What is it usually made of?
hints: The branches are green.
They smell like the forest.
They come from the same tree as the Christmas tree.
questions.fun_fact: The first Advent wreath, made in Hamburg in 1839, was a wooden wheel with lots of small candles and four big ones.

media.credit: Upcomingphotographerscorner · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Upcomingphotographerscorner

questions.description: When bureaucracy decorates for Christmas, it needs a very long label.
questions.question: In East Germany, Christmas decorations were meant to have non-religious names. Which word supposedly came up for the angel?
hints: The word avoids “Weihnachten” and “Engel”.
It plainly describes what an angel has on its back.
Instead of Christmas, it names a point in the calendar: the end of the year.
questions.fun_fact: Whether the word was ever used officially is disputed; it became famous mostly as a joke about East German bureaucracy.

media.credit: Geolina163 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Geolina163

questions.description: The only person whose dirty jacket you're happy to pat on New Year's Eve.
questions.question: He wears black and a top hat, and touching him on New Year's Eve is said to bring luck. What is his job?
hints: He often works high up on rooftops.
His work leaves him covered in soot.
He cleans the flues that smoke from the fireplace goes up.
questions.fun_fact: A clean chimney once prevented house fires and kept the kitchen warm, which is why the sweep was seen as a bringer of luck.

media.credit: Christine Matthews · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Christine Matthews

questions.description: The first breaking news of the Christmas story arrived without a single phone.
questions.question: In the Christmas story, who tells the shepherds in the field that Jesus has been born?
hints: At first the shepherds get a terrible fright.
It comes straight from heaven.
It has wings and often sits at the very top of the Christmas tree.
questions.fun_fact: The word “angel” comes from the Greek “angelos”, which means “messenger”.

media.credit: Matson Collection · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Matson Collection

questions.description: Cookies whose name already gives away half the recipe.
questions.question: Advent cookies cut out with cookie cutters and decorated with icing often have a fat in their name. Which one?
hints: It's a classic baking ingredient.

media.author: Shixart1985

questions.description: Pine trees, lakes and sand: more nature here than headlines.
questions.question: Which German state does this map show? The hole in the middle is not a printing mistake.
hints: It lies in eastern Germany.
The hole is a state of its own.
Its capital is Potsdam, home of Sanssouci Palace.
questions.fun_fact: The Brandenburg Gate isn't in Brandenburg at all but in Berlin; it's named after the road to the town of Brandenburg an der Havel.

media.credit: Grundkarte NordNordWest, Relief Alexrk2 · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Grundkarte NordNordWest, Relief Alexrk2

questions.description: France is right next door, and some things just stuck around in Saarland.
questions.question: It’s named after a French city, it’s a classic in Saarland and it’s often eaten in slices. What is a “Lyoner”?
hints: You buy it at the butcher’s counter.
In Saarland, people also fry it in a pan with potatoes.
Elsewhere it’s often called Fleischwurst.
questions.fun_fact: In Lyon itself, the sausage is hardly known by this name, and where it really comes from is still unclear.

media.credit: Pascal Dihé · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Pascal Dihé

questions.description: Dresden, the Elbe, Baroque style and a church with quite an eventful life story.
questions.question: You’re standing in front of Dresden’s Frauenkirche. What was on this spot for about 50 years before it was rebuilt?
hints: Nothing new was built on this spot in East German times.
The church was destroyed in February 1945.
Many of the old stones were used again when it was rebuilt.
questions.fun_fact: The dark stones in the light-colored walls come from the old church, which makes it look like a jigsaw puzzle.

media.credit: Matthias Frank · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Matthias Frank

questions.description: A furry resident of the capital who never had to go apartment hunting.
questions.question: The bear on Berlin's coat of arms: how many legs is it standing on?
hints: It is black and sticks out its red tongue.
It looks ready for a fight, with its claws stretched forward.
It stands upright, like a person.
questions.fun_fact: The top prize of the Berlin Film Festival is a bear too: the Golden Bear.

media.credit: Thomas Wolf, www.foto-tw.de · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Thomas Wolf, www.foto-tw.de

questions.description: There's so much Baltic Sea air here, they should really start exporting it.
questions.question: How many other German states does Mecklenburg-Vorpommern border?
hints: To the north lies the Baltic Sea, to the east Poland.
To the west it borders Schleswig-Holstein and Lower Saxony.
To the south, only Brandenburg is left.
questions.fun_fact: Mecklenburg-Vorpommern has about 2,000 lakes, including the Müritz, the largest lake that lies entirely within Germany.

media.credit: Siarhei Besarab · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Siarhei Besarab

questions.description: A tower that tells you the time, if you can just count the lights fast enough.
questions.question: The Rheinturm is about 240 m (787 ft) tall, stands next to the state parliament and shows the time with lights. In which city is it?
hints: People here prefer Altbier to Kölsch.
The Königsallee is a famous shopping street here.
This city is the state capital of North Rhine-Westphalia.
questions.fun_fact: The lights on the tower's shaft are said to form the world's largest decimal clock.

media.credit: Dietmar Rabich · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Dietmar Rabich

questions.description: A pastry with its arms crossed and a different name depending on where you are.
questions.question: Who would typically call this pastry a “Brezn”?
hints: People there often call a bread roll a “Semmel”.
The region is in the south of Germany and reaches the Alps.
It’s the state whose capital is Munich.
questions.fun_fact: You can spot a Swabian pretzel by its thin little arms and its fat “belly”.

media.credit: Tamorlan · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Tamorlan

questions.description: It hangs out all day and still has a bad reputation.
questions.question: Bats were once seen as witches’ animals that get tangled in your hair at night. Bats are mammals. What are their wings made of?
hints: Birds and bats fly in very different ways.
The wings are soft and stretchy and fold up like an umbrella.
The wing is a rebuilt hand, and you have its material all over your body too.
questions.fun_fact: Bats don’t get caught in hair: thanks to echolocation, they can even dodge thin threads.

media.credit: W.carter · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: W.carter

questions.description: A broom, a cauldron and a grumpy witch’s cat cooked up this saying together.
questions.question: What do Germans mean when they say “Das ist wie verhext!”?
wrong_answers: Someone is acting like a witch
Something has gone suddenly, eerily quiet
hints: People usually say it when they’re annoyed.
It feels as if someone had put a curse on things.
The key won’t fit, the printer won’t print, the puzzle piece is missing.
questions.fun_fact: In the old days, people really did blame witches when the milk went sour or the butter wouldn’t set.

media.credit: InfosReseaux · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: InfosReseaux

questions.description: A wolf who clearly bit off more than he could chew at dinner.
questions.question: In the Brothers Grimm fairy tale, the big bad wolf eats Little Red Riding Hood and her grandmother. Who gets them both out of his belly?
hints: He hears the wolf snoring loudly.
He spends a lot of time in the forest.
He carries a rifle and wears a green hat.
questions.fun_fact: Afterwards they fill the wolf's belly with heavy stones.

media.credit: F R · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: F R

questions.description: A dance floor the lawn laid out all by itself.
questions.question: Sometimes mushrooms grow in a perfect circle on a meadow. According to legend, when did elves dance there?
hints: Elves don't like being watched by humans.
Elves love soft, silvery light.
The stars are shining in the sky then.
questions.fun_fact: The mushroom ring forms because the fungus's web of threads underground grows a bit further outward every year.

media.credit: User:Mrs skippy · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: User:Mrs skippy

questions.description: A pinch of panic for the kitchen table.
questions.question: Superstition says that if you spill salt, you should quickly throw a pinch of it. Where?
hints: The salt is meant to hit someone lurking behind you.
That someone is the devil.
He sits on the side where your heart beats.
questions.fun_fact: In Leonardo da Vinci’s “The Last Supper,” Judas has knocked over a salt cellar.

media.credit: Jorge Royan · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jorge Royan

questions.description: The magic word after a big “Achoo!”
questions.question: In Germany, someone sneezes and you wish them not to get sick. Which word do you call out?
hints: You say it right after the sneeze.
Lots of Americans say it too.
It's the German word for “health.”
questions.fun_fact: People once believed that a sneeze could let illness or evil spirits slip into the body.

media.credit: Captain MarcusL · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Captain MarcusL

questions.description: A wish machine standing in every meadow.
questions.question: It's white and fluffy, and you blow it away and make a wish. What hangs from each of its tiny parachutes?
hints: The wind carries the tiny parachutes far away.
Where they land, something happens later.
A new dandelion grows from it.
questions.fun_fact: The tiny parachutes of a dandelion puff, the “Pusteblume”, can be carried many kilometers by the wind.

media.credit: Monstieur Kraken · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Monstieur Kraken

questions.description: A bird that has to fill in for somebody else entirely.
questions.question: In old German curses like “Zum Kuckuck!” or “Weiß der Kuckuck!”, the cuckoo stands for someone people didn't want to name. Who?
hints: People feared that saying his name would summon him.
He is said to have horns and a horse's hoof.
He supposedly lives in hell.
questions.fun_fact: German folk belief says you should jingle the coins in your purse when you hear the first cuckoo call in spring, so your money won't run out all year.

media.credit: Tisha Mukherjee · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Tisha Mukherjee

questions.description: A beauty product made for one very special job.
questions.question: Folk belief says witches mixed an ointment in their cauldron and rubbed it on their brooms. What was it for?
hints: They really needed it on Walpurgis Night.
They wanted to travel to the Blocksberg with it.
After that, things went sky-high.
questions.fun_fact: On Walpurgis Night, witches were said to fly to the Brocken in the Harz Mountains, also known as the Blocksberg.

media.author:
