questions.description: The farmers' weather report always had a good eye for color.
questions.question: What does the old German farmers' saying „Grüne Weihnachten, weiße Ostern“ (“green Christmas, white Easter”) predict?
questions.answer: No snow at Christmas, but snow at Easter
wrong_answers: Snow at Christmas, but lots of sun at Easter
Lots of rain in December, lots of sun at Easter
Green fir trees at Christmas, white Easter eggs
hints: It's about the weather on two holidays.
The two holidays sort of swap their looks.
White is what drifts down from the sky in winter.
questions.fun_fact: In much of Germany there's usually no snow at Christmas, so a “green Christmas” is more the rule than the exception.

media.credit: smunster · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: smunster

questions.description: Under the Christmas tree, a shoebox looks more harmless than it really is.
questions.question: According to superstition, you should never give anyone shoes. What will the person do with them otherwise?
hints: Shoes are made for walking, after all.
The shoes carry them in one particular direction.
In the end, the giver is left alone.
questions.fun_fact: As a remedy, the person getting the shoes often hands over a small coin, so the shoes count as bought.

media.credit: No restrictions · Wikimedia Commons

questions.description: Fog, moonlight, longing – and somebody got the wrong century.
questions.question: You walk through a museum room of German Romantic paintings. Which work does NOT belong there?
wrong_answers: “The Monk by the Sea” by Caspar David Friedrich
“The Hülsenbeck Children” by Philipp Otto Runge
“Wanderer above the Sea of Fog” by Caspar David Friedrich
hints: Romanticism flourished from about 1800 to 1840.
One painting was made about 100 years later.
Its painter belonged to the New Objectivity and showed the nightlife of the Weimar Republic.
questions.fun_fact: The “Wanderer above the Sea of Fog” hangs in the Hamburger Kunsthalle – just like Runge's “Hülsenbeck Children”.

media.credit: A.Savin · FAL · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: A.Savin

questions.description: High ceilings, creaky floorboards and a landlord who calls it “charm”.
questions.question: Ceiling decorations like the one in the photo are typical of German Altbau apartments. What are they usually made of?
hints: The material is white and is mixed with water.
It is worked while soft and then hardens.
Doctors use it for hard casts on broken bones.
questions.fun_fact: Many old buildings in German cities date from the Gründerzeit boom around 1900, and their ceilings are often over 3 m (10 ft) high.

media.credit: Globetrotter19 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Globetrotter19

questions.description: A house that looks like a child drew the building plans, and that was the whole idea.
questions.question: This pink building with golden balls and trees on the roof stands in Magdeburg. Which artist designed it?
hints: He was mainly a painter and disliked straight lines.
He came from Vienna.
A colorful apartment building in Vienna is named after him.
questions.fun_fact: The Green Citadel opened in 2005, five years after its creator died; it was his last project.

media.credit: Axel Tschentscher · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Axel Tschentscher

questions.description: Every five years, a town in northern Hesse becomes the center of the world.
questions.question: Since 1955, documenta has been held in Kassel for 100 days, about every five years. What is it?
hints: You walk through halls, parks and museums there.
Joseph Beuys had 7,000 oak trees planted for it.
It is also called the “museum of 100 days.”
questions.fun_fact: For Beuys's work “7000 Oaks,” trees were planted across Kassel from 1982, each next to a basalt column, and the last one went into the ground in 1987.

media.credit: Harmish Khambhaita · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Harmish Khambhaita

questions.description: Probably the most-framed pair of hands in Germany.
questions.question: Prints of Albrecht Dürer's “Praying Hands” hang in many living rooms. In what year was the drawing made?
hints: Dürer lived in Nuremberg during the Renaissance.
A few years earlier, Columbus had reached America.
In the same year, Michelangelo began painting the Sistine Chapel ceiling.
questions.fun_fact: The hands were a study for an altarpiece whose central panel was lost in a fire in 1729, but the drawing survived.

media.credit: Fred Romero from Paris, France · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Fred Romero from Paris, France

questions.description: One color, one rider, and suddenly painting looks completely different.
questions.question: This 1912 almanac bears the name of a Munich artists' group. Who founded it in 1911 together with Franz Marc?
hints: He came from Moscow.
He is seen as one of the inventors of abstract painting.
He wrote the book “Concerning the Spiritual in Art”.
questions.fun_fact: According to Kandinsky, the name came up over coffee: both loved blue, Marc loved horses, and Kandinsky loved riders.

media.credit: Goesseln · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Goesseln

questions.description: Here the gables have more swirls than a wedding cake.
questions.question: Grand buildings in Hameln, Lemgo and Hämelschenburg Castle, built around 1520 to 1620: what is this architectural style called?
hints: The style was influenced by Italy and the Netherlands.
Typical features are decorated gables and bay windows, locally called “Utluchten”.
It is named after the river that Hameln lies on.
questions.fun_fact: A famous example is the Rat Catcher's House in Hameln, where an old inscription recalls the legend of the Pied Piper.

media.credit: Bernd Schwabe in Hannover · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bernd Schwabe in Hannover

questions.description: A hundred meters, a blink of an eye, and in the end a belly flop trimmed in gold.
questions.question: “I sprint for Germany, threw myself across the finish line in Munich in 2022 and became European 100-meter champion.” Who am I?
hints: I come from Westphalia.
At the 2024 Olympics, I won bronze with the relay team.
My last name starts with “Lücken…”.
questions.fun_fact: Lückenkemper fell as she dived across the finish line, but she still got there first.

media.credit: Eckhard Pecher (Arcimboldo) · CC BY 2.5 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Eckhard Pecher (Arcimboldo)

questions.description: Swim, bike, run – and then a week on the couch.
questions.question: Patrick Lange won the Ironman World Championship in 2017, 2018 and 2024, and in 2018 was the first to finish it in under eight hours. On which island?
hints: The island is volcanic.
The swim is in the Pacific Ocean.
The race starts in Kona.
questions.fun_fact: After his 2018 win, Lange proposed to his girlfriend right at the finish line.

media.credit: Alex Lomas · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Alex Lomas

questions.description: Others retire; she'd rather do one more lap on the ice.
questions.question: Claudia Pechstein competed at her eighth Olympic Games in Beijing in 2022. In what year were her first?
hints: Back then, the Summer and Winter Games were still held in the same year.
The Games took place in Albertville, France.
They were the first Winter Games of reunified Germany.
questions.fun_fact: At Beijing 2022, Pechstein, at nearly 50, carried the German flag at the opening ceremony.

media.credit: Arne Müseler · CC BY-SA 3.0 de · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Arne Müseler

questions.description: A whole swimming pool full of gold, and nobody had to dive for it.
questions.question: Kristin Otto, later a presenter on German TV channel ZDF, swam for East Germany at the 1988 Seoul Olympics. How many gold medals did she win there?
hints: No other woman won more at those Games.
At the time, it was a record for a woman at a single Olympics.
It was half a dozen.
questions.fun_fact: Otto won her gold medals in three different strokes: freestyle, backstroke and butterfly.

media.credit: Arne Müseler · CC BY-SA 3.0 de · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Arne Müseler

questions.description: It roars louder here than at a lawnmower race.
questions.question: This racetrack in Baden-Württemberg, near Mannheim, is named after its town and has often hosted Formula 1. Which one?
hints: The town is close to Heidelberg.
Part of its grandstands is called the “Motodrom”.
The name starts with “Hocken…”.
questions.fun_fact: Until 2001, the track ran deep into the forest; in 2002 it was made much shorter.

media.credit: Morio · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Morio

questions.description: The thing that helps more than any excuse after you fall off your bike.
questions.question: I'm small, I stick to scraped knees, and I have a soft pad in the middle. Which brand name do many people know me by?
hints: I belong in every first aid kit.
My name starts like the old trading league of Hamburg and Lübeck.
Hanse + Pflaster (German for “bandage”) almost makes my name.
questions.fun_fact: Hansaplast, Nivea and Tesa all come from the same Hamburg company: Beiersdorf.

media.credit: Saimmx · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Saimmx

questions.description: A slogan that makes every piggy bank squeal with joy.
questions.question: An electronics store ad on TV uses the slogan “Geiz ist geil!”. Which decade are you most likely in?
hints: The Deutsche Mark was already gone by then.
The campaign ran while the euro was still brand new.
It started in 2002.
questions.fun_fact: The Jung von Matt agency came up with the slogan for the Saturn chain, and it ran until about 2007.

media.credit: Intel Free Press · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Intel Free Press

questions.description: A lifesaver for anyone who misspells a word in the middle of a school dictation.
questions.question: It has two ends: one makes blue fountain pen ink disappear, the other writes over it. What is this pen called in Germany?
hints: It's in almost every pencil case in German primary school.
It goes with the fountain pen the way an eraser goes with a pencil.
Its name sounds like it finishes off the ink.
questions.fun_fact: The erasing end bleaches the blue dye chemically, which is why it usually doesn't work on black ink.

media.author: Petar Milošević

questions.description: Chew on one of these and a classroom goes quiet for a moment… almost.
questions.question: Which of these candies is NOT made by Maoam?

The odd one out comes from the big company that owns Maoam today.
It's an animal, and its name has the color of treasure in it.
questions.fun_fact: Maoam has belonged to Haribo since 1986, so the Goldbären and Maoam are siblings.

media.author: martinak15 from United States

questions.description: Even people with GPS get lost in here.

hints: It looks just like the other path tiles and passes from player to player.
You use it on every turn, before you move your piece.
Afterwards, a whole row slides along by one space.
questions.fun_fact: The game was invented by Max Kobbert and came out from Ravensburger in 1986.

media.author: Joseolgon

questions.description: A club where the fans don't just sing, they also swing a shovel.
questions.question: When the An der Alten Försterei stadium was rebuilt in 2008/09, Union Berlin fans helped for free. About how many were there?
hints: More than would fit in a school gym.
Together they put in about 140,000 hours of work.
The number is between 2,000 and 2,500.
questions.fun_fact: Union fans are called “die Eisernen” (the Iron Ones), and at Christmas tens of thousands of them sing carols together in the stadium.

media.author: Arne Müseler

questions.description: The rule that gets argued about at every Stammtisch in the country.
questions.question: The linesman's flag goes up, the whistle blows, and the goal doesn't count: “Offside!” What did the attacker do wrong?

wrong_answers: He touched the ball with his hand
He knocked an opponent over from behind
He played the ball over the sideline
hints: The rule was already part of the early rules of the game in the 1800s.
The rule stops strikers from simply waiting next to the other team's goal.
He was closer to the goal than the second-to-last defender.
questions.fun_fact: You can never be offside in your own half.

media.author: Rick Dikeman

hints: A draw gets you less.
A draw is worth exactly one point.
It's the number of sides of a triangle.
questions.fun_fact: Until 1995, a win in the Bundesliga was worth only two points.

media.credit: ticketsluxury · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons

questions.description: The most expensive piece of paper in many fans' wallets.

hints: There are 18 teams in the Bundesliga.
Each team plays every opponent once at home and once away.
It is exactly half of 34.
questions.fun_fact: At some clubs, fans spend many years on a waiting list for a season ticket.

media.author: Lewis Clarke

questions.description: Where the shin guards are almost as big as the players.
questions.question: German youth soccer runs from the G-Jugend up to the A-Jugend. The E-Jugend is for children aged…
hints: The G-Jugend is for the very youngest.
The E-Jugend is also called U11.
They are kids in third and fourth grade.
questions.fun_fact: In the E-Jugend, teams usually play with seven players on a smaller field.

media.author: Javierme Javier Mediavilla Ezquibela

questions.description: A coin that gets around more than any backpacker.
questions.question: In the circle game „Taler, Taler, du musst wandern“, an old silver coin travels around. Which modern currency is named after it?
hints: This currency is known all over the world today.
In Dutch, “Taler” became “daalder”.
It's what people pay with in the USA.
questions.fun_fact: The name Taler comes from the “Joachimsthaler”, a silver coin from the town of Joachimsthal in Bohemia.

media.author: Unknown / Commissioned by Ulrich, Duke of Württemberg

questions.description: A crime under the palm trees, and the loot is rock hard.
questions.question: In the children's song “Wer hat die Kokosnuss geklaut?” (“Who stole the coconut?”), which animals shout it together as a whole gang?

At the zoo, their house often has lots of climbing ropes.
They swing from branch to branch and like bananas.
questions.fun_fact: Botanically, a coconut isn't a nut at all but a drupe, a fruit with a stone inside.

media.credit: Ivar Leidus · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ivar Leidus

questions.description: If you have no scissors on you, just grab a sword.
questions.question: In the song “Sankt Martin ritt durch Schnee und Wind”, Martin cuts his cloak with his sword. Into how many pieces?

A freezing beggar sits in the snow, and Martin gives him some of his cloak.
One piece for Martin, one piece for the beggar.
questions.fun_fact: The word “chapel” (German “Kapelle”) comes from Martin's cloak (Latin “cappa”), later kept as a relic in a small prayer room.

media.credit: PAUL FARMER · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: PAUL FARMER

questions.description: Ten little fellows who can never sit still. Sound familiar?
questions.question: They wiggle back and forth, crawl up and down, and hide at the end. What are the “Zehn kleine Zappelmänner” (ten little wiggle men)?

You always have them with you.
You have five of them on each hand.
questions.fun_fact: At the end of the game, the wiggle men usually hide behind your back or inside your fist.

media.author: State Library of Queensland, Australia

questions.description: A bush you sit under, shout at, and then run away from in a flash.
questions.question: In “Ringel, Ringel, Reihe”, the children sit “unterm Hollerbusch”. What bush is that?

Its berries are small and almost black.
Its usual German name sounds almost like “Holler”.

media.credit: Shixart1985 · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Shixart1985

questions.description: A tree that delivers more at bedtime than any fruit stand.
questions.question: In the lullaby “Schlaf, Kindlein, schlaf”, the mother shakes the little tree. What falls down from it?
hints: Meanwhile, the father is looking after the sheep.
It goes very well with falling asleep.
You have it at night with your eyes closed.
questions.fun_fact: In another verse, sheep wander across the sky: the little stars are the lambs, and the moon is the shepherd.

media.credit: Narender9 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Narender9

questions.description: The longest nap in fairy-tale history, and no alarm clock allowed.
questions.question: In the circle game song “Dornröschen war ein schönes Kind”, the wicked fairy casts a curse. How many years must Dornröschen sleep?

This stretch of time is also called a century.
questions.fun_fact: In the Brothers Grimm tale, not only Dornröschen falls asleep but the whole castle, even the flies on the wall.

media.author: Richard Humphrey

questions.description: Five fingers, one fruit harvest and one very greedy little guy.
questions.question: Finish the German finger rhyme: “Das ist der Daumen, der schüttelt die …” What does the thumb shake?
hints: It's a fruit.
It's usually purple or blue.
In German, the word rhymes with “Daumen”.
questions.fun_fact: At the end of the rhyme, the little finger eats up all the plums by himself.

media.credit: Shixart1985 · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Shixart1985

questions.description: A crime case where the evidence literally falls from the sky.
questions.question: A little mole asks lots of animals who pooped on his head. Two flies solve the case. Which animal was it?

Its name is Hans-Heinerich and it barks.
questions.fun_fact: In the end the mole gets his revenge and drops a little “sausage” of his own on the culprit’s head.

I stood for “glasnost” and “perestroika”.
I was the last leader of the Soviet Union.
questions.fun_fact: Gorbachev never said the line in exactly those words: the short version probably came from his spokesman, Gennady Gerasimov.

The man I'm named after died a year after me, in 1953.
I'm named after the Soviet Union's ruler at the time.
questions.fun_fact: Historians still argue whether the offer was serious or only meant to disrupt West Germany's ties to the West.

The FDJ flag was this color too.
questions.fun_fact: The sun on the sleeve was the emblem of the FDJ, the Free German Youth.

He came from Leipzig and had trained as a carpenter.
He is the man who said “No one has the intention of building a wall.”
questions.fun_fact: The former Council of State building in Berlin now houses a private business school.

questions.question: I was founded on October 7, 1949, a few months after my western neighbor. My holiday was called “Day of the Republic”. Who am I?
hints: I was in Central Europe.
I was a member of the Warsaw Pact.
My capital was East Berlin.
questions.fun_fact: Just six days before the GDR, on October 1, 1949, the People's Republic of China was proclaimed.

A yellow sign with a post horn shows the way.

Someone like this thinks long and hard before spending anything.
It's the opposite of throwing money around.

questions.description: The only pig that looks sad when its tummy is empty.
questions.question: It's pink, made of china and has a slot in its back. What do you put into this pig?
hints: You often find it in a kid's bedroom.
When you shake it, it jingles.
Later you can buy something with what's inside.
questions.fun_fact: In German, “slaughtering” your piggy bank (das Sparschwein schlachten) doesn't hurt it at all: it just means taking all the coins out.

media.credit: Shixart1985 · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Shixart1985

questions.description: Buy it, rip it open, be amazed, and sometimes be a little disappointed.
questions.question: This colorful sealed bag is sold at the kiosk. It holds candy and a small toy, but you don't know which one beforehand. What is it called?
hints: The exciting part is the surprise.
There's often a sticker or a little plastic figure inside.
The first part of its name means “miracle” or “wonder”.
questions.fun_fact: The idea is a bit like the Kinder Surprise egg: there, too, you don't know which toy is inside until you unwrap it.

media.credit: Christoffre · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Christoffre

questions.description: Long before delivery apps, there was a memory that knew exactly which milk you wanted.
questions.question: I know every customer by name and sometimes let them pay later. Small corner shops are named after me. Who am I?
hints: I sell flour, milk and candy from big glass jars.
Supermarkets have pushed shops like mine almost out of business.
I'm related to you: I'm your mother's or father's sister.
questions.fun_fact: Small village shops are making a comeback: many are now run by the villagers themselves as cooperatives.

media.credit: Scott Edmunds · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Scott Edmunds

questions.description: A smile, a “Would you like one?”, and the kid is in a great mood for the rest of the shopping trip.
questions.question: When shopping, kids are often given a free slice of sausage like this one. Who gives it to them?
hints: He stands behind a glass counter.
He often wears a white apron.
He's the one who sells you schnitzel and sausages.
questions.fun_fact: The “Kinderscheibe” (kid's slice) is usually Fleischwurst or Gelbwurst, and many adults still remember exactly how it tasted.

media.credit: Roy Zuo · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Roy Zuo

questions.description: A topic the Bundesbank looks at very closely, and even touches.
questions.question: Passing it on is a crime. The Bundesbank says you can spot it with “Feel – Look – Tilt”. What is it?
hints: The police hunt for the people who make it.
Real bills have a hologram and a watermark instead.
In everyday German, such bills are called “Blüten”.
questions.fun_fact: If you accidentally take a “Blüte”, you don't get your money back: it has to be handed in to the police or a bank.

media.credit: spacepleb · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: spacepleb

questions.description: The smallest money in your wallet carries a little piece of forest around with it.
questions.question: These leaves are shown on the German 1, 2 and 5 cent coins. Which tree do they come from?
hints: The old pfennig already showed this tree.
It is seen as a typically German tree and can live to a great age.
Wild boars love its nuts with their little caps.
questions.fun_fact: A cent isn't made of pure copper but of steel with a thin copper coating, which is why it sticks to a magnet.

media.credit: Wald-Burger8 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Wald-Burger8

questions.description: A device that has a lot more to do in winter than in summer.
questions.question: Why do many rented apartments have this small device on the radiator?
questions.answer: It records usage for the heating bill
wrong_answers: It lets air out of the radiator
It warns when the air is too dry
hints: It gets read once a year, these days often by radio.
That way one bill can be split fairly among all the tenants in the building.
The result ends up in the yearly statement of extra housing costs.
questions.fun_fact: Older heat cost allocators have a small tube of liquid that slowly evaporates with the heat.

media.credit: Georg Zumstrull · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Georg Zumstrull

questions.description: An earworm that has been wearing hiking boots for almost 200 years.
questions.question: This folk song dates from 1844. In it, the water, the wheels and even the stones go wandering, and it's a school-trip classic. Which song is it?
hints: The singer first learns to wander from the water.
The wheels and stones belong to a workshop by a stream.
The trade in the song's title grinds grain into flour.
questions.fun_fact: The words are by Wilhelm Müller, whose poems Franz Schubert set to music in “Die schöne Müllerin”.

media.credit: Leonhard Lenz · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Leonhard Lenz

questions.description: In summer, many a mountain turns into a giant playground.
questions.question: I wind down a hillside, made of steel or plastic. I don't need snow: you zoom down me into the valley on small sleds with wheels. What am I?
hints: You ride alone or in pairs and do your own braking.
In winter you'd ride down me on a real sled.
My name gives away the season when I'm the most fun.
questions.fun_fact: On many summer toboggan runs you zoom down at up to about 40 km/h (25 mph), braking with a lever on the sled.

media.credit: Simon Broccard · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Simon Broccard

questions.description: Bavarian mountains have family names, and this is a bit of family-tree research.
questions.question: Zugspitze is to the Wetterstein range as Kampenwand is to …?
hints: The Kampenwand is in Upper Bavaria, near Aschau.
From the summit you look down on a large lake.
That lake is also called the “Bavarian Sea”.
questions.fun_fact: The Kampenwand is about 1,669 m (5,476 ft) high and has one of the largest summit crosses in the Bavarian Alps.

media.credit: Andreas Kretschmer · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Andreas Kretschmer

questions.description: A town that took a direct hit from outer space.
questions.question: Nördlingen lies in a crater made by an asteroid about 15 million years ago. Roughly how wide is it?
hints: A whole town plus villages fits inside it.
From Nördlingen, the crater rim only shows as a distant line of hills.
Crossing it by bike would take about an hour.
questions.fun_fact: In 1970, Apollo 14 astronauts practiced rock studies for the Moon in the Ries crater.

media.credit: Wolkenkratzer · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Wolkenkratzer

questions.description: Here you're old enough at 16 for the ballot box, but still too young for a driver's license.
questions.question: Which German state was the first to let 16-year-olds vote in its state parliament election?
hints: It's a city-state.
It is made up of two cities that are separate from each other.
This is where the four animal musicians in the Grimm fairy tale were headed.
questions.fun_fact: In the 2011 state election, Bremen became the first place in Germany where 16-year-olds could help elect a state parliament.

media.credit: W.carter · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: W.carter

questions.description: At 14, German teens get more say than some parents would like.
questions.question: When you turn 14 in Germany, you become “religionsmündig”. What does that mean?
wrong_answers: You must start paying church tax
You may get married in church
hints: It has to do with the freedom of religion in the Basic Law.
Before this age, parents usually decide.
From this age you can, for example, join or leave a church on your own.
questions.fun_fact: Already at 12, a child in Germany can no longer be raised in a different faith against their will.

media.credit: Radomianin · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Radomianin

questions.description: For decades, this job only ever came with a tie.
questions.question: In what year did Angela Merkel become the first woman to serve as Germany's chancellor?
hints: It was in the first decade of the 21st century.
Her predecessor was Gerhard Schröder.
The year after, Germany hosted the World Cup known as the “Sommermärchen” (summer fairy tale).
questions.fun_fact: Angela Merkel governed for 16 years, almost exactly as long as Helmut Kohl.

media.credit: Norbert Nagel · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Norbert Nagel

questions.description: A top job whose name originally sounds more like fetching the coffee.
questions.question: My title comes from the Latin word for “servant.” The chancellor proposes me, and I run areas like finance or health. Who am I?
hints: I am appointed by the federal president.
Together with the chancellor, I make up the federal government.
I sit at the cabinet table and run my own ministry.
questions.fun_fact: The Latin “minister” is the opposite of “magister”: one serves, the other is the master.

media.credit: Cabinet Secretariat · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Cabinet Secretariat

questions.description: A date in the Bundestag's calendar when nobody cracks jokes.
questions.question: Since 1996, which day has been Germany's Day of Remembrance for the Victims of National Socialism?
hints: A federal president declared this day of remembrance.
The United Nations marks it as an international day of remembrance.
On this day in 1945, the Auschwitz camp was liberated.
questions.fun_fact: Federal President Roman Herzog proclaimed the day of remembrance on January 3, 1996.

media.credit: Photo: Andreas Praefcke · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Photo: Andreas Praefcke

questions.description: So nobody gets to decide everything alone, just like siblings cutting a cake.
questions.question: The Bundestag passes laws, the government carries them out, and the courts check both. What is this principle called?
hints: It sets the legislative, executive and judicial branches apart.
The Frenchman Montesquieu made the idea famous.
The power of the state is split among three branches.
questions.fun_fact: Some people jokingly call the press the “fourth estate” because it keeps an eye on the other three.

media.credit: Wladyslaw Sojka · FAL · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Wladyslaw Sojka

questions.description: A Latin-sounding word that comes up in Brussels more often than rain.
questions.question: The principle of subsidiarity is in Germany's Basic Law and in the EU treaties. What does it require?
questions.answer: What a smaller level can handle, it handles itself
wrong_answers: The federal government always outranks the states
The state funds all non-profit associations
Important laws need a public referendum
hints: The idea comes from Catholic social teaching.
It decides how tasks are shared between the EU, the federal government, the states and local towns.
Only when the lower level can't cope does the higher one step in.
questions.fun_fact: The word comes from the Latin “subsidium”, meaning reserve or help, the same root as the English word “subsidy”.

media.credit: Tournasol7 · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Tournasol7

questions.description: Sometimes half isn't enough in politics, and then you have to win over a whole lot of people.
questions.question: Here and in the Bundesrat, this needs two thirds of the votes in each. What for?
hints: It's about something that is meant to be very well protected.
No government should be able to do this with just a simple majority.
It's about the German constitution.
questions.fun_fact: Under the “eternity clause”, some principles, such as human dignity, can't be abolished even with a two-thirds majority.

media.credit: Photo: Andreas Praefcke · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Photo: Andreas Praefcke

questions.description: Before the ball starts rolling, everyone sings first, even the people who can't sing.
questions.question: Before an international match, a second anthem is played along with the German one. Who is it for?
hints: In an international match, two countries play each other.
Every country has its own anthem.
The players on the other side sing along to it.
questions.fun_fact: At home games, the visitors' anthem is usually played first, then the hosts' anthem.

media.credit: ticketsluxury · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: ticketsluxury

questions.description: For everyone who said as a kid: “That's unfair, I'm going all the way to the top!”
questions.question: If you think the state has violated your basic rights, you can take me to Karlsruhe, no lawyer needed. What am I?
hints: Anyone in Germany may file me.
As a rule, I cost nothing.
I end up at the highest court for the Basic Law.
questions.fun_fact: Every year thousands of complaints arrive in Karlsruhe, but only a small share of them succeed.

media.credit: Carsten Steger · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Carsten Steger

questions.description: One slip of paper, two columns, and a whole lot of ballpoint pens every four years.
questions.question: What is the left column on this Bundestag election ballot for?
questions.answer: Choosing a person in your own district
wrong_answers: Choosing a party for all of Germany
hints: The left column is called the Erststimme (first vote).
It lists the names of people from your area.
For this, Germany is split into almost 300 areas.
questions.fun_fact: For the Bundestag election, Germany is divided into 299 electoral districts.

media.credit: Bundeswahlleiter · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bundeswahlleiter

questions.description: A summer evening when all of Germany crossed its fingers until they hurt.
questions.question: Germany's women lost the Euro 2022 final 2–1 after extra time. The winners were the hosts and took their first major title. Which country?
hints: The tournament took place in July, in the middle of a heat wave.
The final was played in its capital city.
That's where the famous Wembley Stadium stands.
questions.fun_fact: 87,192 people watched the final in the stadium, more than at any European Championship before, men's tournaments included.

media.credit: Krazytea · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Krazytea

questions.description: Above the eagle, the sky gets a little more crowded with every title.
questions.question: Germany wears a star for every World Cup title; the fourth came in Brazil in 2014. In which country was the very first won?
hints: The first title came in 1954.
There's a famous movie about the final with “Miracle” in its title.
The final was played in the city of Bern.
questions.fun_fact: In the 1954 final, Germany beat a Hungary team thought to be unbeatable 3–2, after losing to them 8–3 in the group stage.

media.credit: Joe Mabel · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Joe Mabel

questions.description: Two countries, one ball, and neither wants to give it up.
questions.question: At Germany's first international match in 1908, how many players were on the field at kickoff, not counting the referee?
hints: Two teams play against each other.
Think of one team's lineup: goalkeeper, defense, midfield and attack.
Each team has eleven players.
questions.fun_fact: Germany lost that first international match in Basel in 1908 to Switzerland, 5–3.

media.credit: MIKI Yoshihito · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: MIKI Yoshihito

questions.description: A hairstyle as legendary as his shots from the penalty spot.
questions.question: This player scored for Germany in the 1974 and 1982 World Cup finals. Who is it?
hints: He started out as a defender and later played in midfield.
In the 1974 final, he scored from the penalty spot.
He played for FC Bayern and Real Madrid and had an afro and a full beard.
questions.fun_fact: Breitner is one of the few players who scored in two different World Cup finals, alongside names like Pelé and Zinédine Zidane.

media.credit: ANSA · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: ANSA

questions.description: When the weather decides the textbook is more of a suggestion.
questions.question: Cold fog hangs in the valley, while on the mountain above the sun shines and it's warmer. What is this kind of weather called?
hints: Normally it gets colder the higher you go.
Here it's the other way round: warmer above than below.
The name comes from the Latin word for “turning upside down”.
questions.fun_fact: In this kind of weather, smog gets stuck in valleys and cities because the warm layer above acts like a lid.

media.credit: Little Mountain 5 · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Little Mountain 5

questions.description: The most beautiful word a thermometer ever came up with.
questions.question: When it gets very hot in summer, Germany sometimes has “Hitzefrei”. Who gets to go home early?
hints: It usually happens by late morning.
Whether it happens is usually decided by someone in charge on site.
Classes are canceled for the rest of the day.
questions.fun_fact: Each German state sets its own rules for Hitzefrei, and usually the school principal makes the call.

media.credit: Pere Serafi · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Pere Serafi

questions.description: A price tag for something you can't even see.
questions.question: Since 2021, Germans pay an extra charge per metric ton of a greenhouse gas when they buy fuel or heat their homes. It makes climate-harming things cost more. What is it called?
hints: The charge goes up with the amount of exhaust gas.
It means the gas that forms when gasoline, heating oil and natural gas are burned.
The name contains the chemical formula of carbon dioxide.
questions.fun_fact: When it started in 2021, one metric ton of CO2 cost 25 euros in Germany.

media.credit: Mutney · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Mutney

questions.description: A weather report with feathers, no app or satellite needed.
questions.question: Listen: an old weather saying claims that when this bird flies low, rain is coming soon. Which bird is it?
hints: It likes to build its nest in barns or under the edges of roofs.
In the fall, it flies all the way to Africa.
It has a forked tail.
questions.fun_fact: The saying has some truth to it: in damp air, insects fly lower, and the swallows chase after them.

media.credit: Sharadapte · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Sharadapte

background.credit: Vyacheslav Argenberg · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
background.author: Vyacheslav Argenberg

questions.description: When the sky plays the drums and brings its own flashlight.
questions.question: In which season does Germany get the most thunderstorms?
hints: Thunderstorms need warm, humid air.
They often come after a hot, muggy day.
It's the season of the long school break.
questions.fun_fact: You can estimate how far away a storm is from the gap between lightning and thunder: three seconds is about one kilometer (about five seconds per mile).

media.credit: Sheba_Also 43,000 photos · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Sheba_Also 43,000 photos

questions.description: A month that flips a coin every morning.
questions.question: “April, April, der macht, was er will” (April does whatever it wants): what weather is NOT typical for April in Germany?
hints: The saying describes weather that keeps changing.
In April, winter often isn't quite over yet.
This is more likely in the middle of summer.
questions.fun_fact: In April, cold polar air and warm air from the south often still collide over Germany, which is why the weather changes so fast.

media.credit: Juandev · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Juandev

questions.description: Hamburg has more than a port and the Elbe: it also owns a few piles of sand in the North Sea.
questions.question: Hamburg Wadden Sea National Park includes islands that belong to the city of Hamburg. Which island does NOT belong to Hamburg?
hints: Three of these islands lie off the mouth of the Elbe near Cuxhaven.
The island you want lies far out in the open sea.
It is known for its red cliffs and the rock pillar “Lange Anna”.
questions.fun_fact: At low tide, you can ride from Cuxhaven to Neuwerk in a horse-drawn carriage straight across the mudflats.

media.credit: Olga Ernst · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Olga Ernst

questions.description: German has more words for bad weather than for a good mood.
questions.question: “Es schüttet wie aus Eimern” means it's pouring with rain. Which German saying does NOT mean heavy rain?
hints: You're looking for a saying where it can stay dry.
It's about air, not water.
You'd say it when the window and the door are both open.
questions.fun_fact: “Es zieht wie Hechtsuppe” describes a strong draft, and where the saying comes from is still argued about today.

media.credit: ©Mohamed Hozyen · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: ©Mohamed Hozyen

questions.description: Ice cubes falling from the sky, but sadly not for your lemonade.
questions.question: On July 12, 1984, a hailstorm hit a big German city and caused the country's most costly insurance damage up to then. Which city was it?
hints: The city is in the south of Germany.
The storm came in from the foothills of the Alps.
The city is famous for Oktoberfest.
questions.fun_fact: Some of the hailstones were as big as tennis balls and smashed countless roofs and car windows.

media.credit: Shixart1985 · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Shixart1985

questions.description: Small but mighty: these fruits have more flavor than their big relatives from the supermarket.
questions.question: You find these tiny red fruits at the edge of the forest in summer. What are they?
hints: You can eat them straight off the plant.
Their big relatives grow in pick-your-own fields.
They're the tiny wild cousins of a fruit people love to dip in chocolate.
questions.fun_fact: The tiny seeds on the outside of a strawberry are actually the plant's real fruits.

media.credit: Ivar Leidus · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ivar Leidus

questions.description: Small, blue-black and wrapped in so many prickles that you think twice before reaching in.
questions.question: These berries grow on a prickly evergreen shrub with needles. What have Germans long used them for?
questions.answer: As a spice for sauerkraut and game
hints: You don't eat them on their own; they're quite bitter.
They often go into the same pot as bay leaves.
A venison roast or Sauerbraten would be only half as good without them.
questions.fun_fact: Botanically, juniper berries aren't berries at all but tiny cones whose scales have grown together.

media.credit: W.carter · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: W.carter

questions.description: Anyone sneaking into the woods at dawn with a basket and a knife won't reveal their favorite spot, not even to their own grandma.
questions.question: I'm yellow like egg yolk, smell a bit like apricot and grow in moss. Germans say a worthless person “isn't worth one of me.” What am I?
hints: I'm an edible mushroom.
Under my cap I have no true gills, only ridges.
In Bavaria I'm also called “Reherl”.
questions.fun_fact: Chanterelles are almost impossible to farm, so nearly all the ones you can buy come from wild forests.

media.credit: Matthew T Rader · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Matthew T Rader

questions.description: It doesn’t shed, it hardly pokes, and every December it moves into the living room.
questions.question: This fir is Germany’s most popular Christmas tree. Which mountain region does it originally come from?
hints: Its name is misleading: it has nothing to do with the north.
Its home lies between the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea.
The country of Georgia is there.
questions.fun_fact: It is named after the Finnish naturalist Alexander von Nordmann, who discovered it in the Caucasus in the 19th century.

media.credit: Zeynel Cebeci · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Zeynel Cebeci

questions.description: Every kindergarten's favorite craft supply in the fall.
questions.question: What is this cone from a conifer made of?
hints: It opens up in dry weather.
The seeds sit between its parts.
The parts overlap like roof tiles.
questions.fun_fact: You almost never find true fir cones on the ground: they fall apart up in the tree, so the cones in the forest mostly come from spruces.

media.credit: Arthur T. LaBar · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Arthur T. LaBar

questions.description: A job where the end of the workday starts with a loud crash.
questions.question: I work in the forest with an ax and a saw and shout “Timber!”. In the fairy tale, Hansel and Gretel’s father is one of us. Who am I?
hints: I don’t need a gun.
I bring tree trunks out of the forest.
My name says what I do with the wood.
questions.fun_fact: Today, giant machines called harvesters often fell trees in the forest and strip off their branches in just a few seconds.

media.credit: Kouya · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Kouya

questions.description: Without this side dish, many a bratwurst would feel pretty lonely on the plate.
questions.question: Which vegetable is this typical German dish made from?
hints: It's a kind of cabbage.
The cabbage is finely shredded and left to ferment with salt.
The head of this cabbage is pale and has smooth leaves.
questions.fun_fact: In southern Germany, “Kraut” is simply another word for cabbage, which is how sauerkraut got its name.

media.credit: avlxyz · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Flickr via Openverse
media.author: avlxyz

questions.description: A record label whose name looks like someone swallowed the space bar while typing.
questions.question: I'm a Berlin DJ who founded the label BPitch Control in 1999 and released Paul Kalkbrenner and Modeselektor there. Who am I?
hints: I've been playing techno in Berlin since the 1990s.
One of my albums is called “Berlinette”.
My stage name sounds like a creature from outer space.
questions.fun_fact: Paul Kalkbrenner's hit “Sky and Sand” from the film “Berlin Calling” came out on BPitch Control.

media.credit: Nikkole Lulu (nikkolodeon) from Hamilton, New Zealand · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Nikkole Lulu (nikkolodeon) from Hamilton, New Zealand

questions.description: The moment when even Dad throws his arms in the air at a wedding.
questions.question: At techno festivals the tension rises, the music thins out, it goes quiet for a second, then the bass and beat slam back in. What is this moment called?
hints: It often comes right after the so-called “build-up”.
Lots of people jump into the air at exactly this moment.
The same word is used for a single bead of rain.
questions.fun_fact: Some producers spend hours working on just the few seconds before the big moment.

media.credit: PinkBeachPlanet · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: PinkBeachPlanet

questions.description: Music for people who find a three-minute song far too rushed.
questions.question: Klaus Schulze once played drums in Tangerine Dream; in the 1970s both made long synthesizer pieces with sequencers. What is this style called?
hints: The name sounds like lessons, but it has nothing to do with classrooms.
It is named after the city where Schulze and Tangerine Dream got started.
Back then, this city was split in two by a wall.
questions.fun_fact: Klaus Schulze's pieces were often so long that a single one filled a whole side of a record.

media.credit: Pete Brown · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Pete Brown

questions.description: Up here the air is thin, the bass is heavy and everyday life is very far away.
questions.question: What is the name of the dance floor upstairs in Berlin's Berghain club, where mostly house music plays?
hints: It sits right above the club's big techno floor.
Photos by Wolfgang Tillmans hang on its walls.
The name joins a word for a wide view and a place where you get drinks.
questions.fun_fact: When the blinds go up for a moment in the morning and sunlight comes in, the whole room often cheers.

media.credit: Oh-Berlin.com · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Oh-Berlin.com

questions.description: A laid-back reggae song suddenly became something the whole world jumped around to.
questions.question: Which German DJ turned OMI's reggae song “Cheerleader” into a remix that hit No. 1 in the US in 2015?
hints: He comes from northern Germany.
He was only 20 years old at the time.
The same year he also had a hit with “Ain't Nobody (Loves Me Better)”.
questions.fun_fact: The original version of “Cheerleader” came out back in 2012 and stayed almost unknown for a long time.

media.credit: Dan Stark dan_stark · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Dan Stark dan_stark

questions.description: The most important price check ever shouted across a dance floor.
questions.question: I'm the frontman of a Hamburg techno band, I have platinum blond hair, and in 1998 I asked “How Much Is the Fish?”. Who am I?
hints: My band shares its name with a small motorbike.
My trademark is the shout “Hyper Hyper!”.
My stage name ends with a double “x”.
questions.fun_fact: The song's melody comes from the Dutch song “Zeven dagen lang” by the band Bots.

media.credit: Dietmar Rabich · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Dietmar Rabich

questions.description: At court around 1700, the rule was simple: if you were important, you had to look important.
questions.question: This is how fine gentlemen looked at German royal courts around 1700. What is this man wearing on his head?
hints: King Louis XIV of France made this fashion famous.
You could put it on and take it off again in the evening.
It was made from human, goat or horse hair and was often powdered white.
questions.fun_fact: In German, the huge curly ones were called “Allongeperücken”, from the French “allonger”, meaning to lengthen.

questions.description: A man who preferred fighting with books to fighting with fists.
questions.question: I wrote fables, worked as a librarian in Wolfenbüttel, and put a Prussian major on stage in “Minna von Barnhelm”. Who am I?
hints: I belong to the Enlightenment, not to Romanticism.
I was born in 1729 in Kamenz, Saxony.
The tragedy “Emilia Galotti” is mine too.
questions.fun_fact: “Minna von Barnhelm”, from 1767, is seen as one of the first great German comedies.

media.author: Dguendel

questions.description: Two names straight out of a nursery rhyme, but the fun soon stopped.

hints: It led to one of the first big inflations in Germany.
A pair of scales played an important part.
Good money was melted down and turned into worse money.
questions.fun_fact: Back then, “kippen” meant clipping coins, and “wippen” came from the seesawing of the scales as heavy coins were picked out.

media.credit: Unknown authorUnknown author · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Unknown authorUnknown author

questions.description: Two little rascals who would drive any village up the wall.
questions.question: How many pranks do Max and Moritz play in Wilhelm Busch's picture story?
hints: The picture story came out in 1865.
Their victims include Widow Bolte, Tailor Böck and Teacher Lämpel.
There are as many pranks as there are days in a week.
questions.fun_fact: “Max und Moritz” is seen as one of the forerunners of today's comics.

media.credit: Jay Pea · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jay Pea

questions.description: In the end, one man was left with nothing but an island in the Atlantic and a lot of free time.
questions.question: You're standing on the battlefield of Waterloo, where Napoleon lost in 1815. Which troops did NOT fight against him here?
hints: The battlefield lies south of Brussels.
Wellington got help just in time from Blücher and his army.
The Tsar's army was still far away at the time.
questions.fun_fact: In Prussia, it was long called the “Battle of Belle Alliance”, after an inn on the battlefield.

media.credit: Myrabella · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Myrabella

questions.description: A few hammer blows, and Europe was never the same again.
questions.question: On October 31, 1517, Luther is said to have posted his theses in Wittenberg. Which Christians came out of the movement he started?
hints: That's why October 31 is a public holiday in several German states.

In Germany they are called “evangelisch.”
questions.fun_fact: Historians still argue about whether Luther really nailed the theses to the church door with a hammer.

questions.description: A day off school for a victory: history class you get to celebrate.

hints: It celebrated a victory in the Franco-Prussian War of 1870.
At Sedan, Emperor Napoleon III was taken prisoner.
The day fell at the very start of the ninth month.
questions.fun_fact: Sedan Day never became an official holiday for the whole Empire, yet it was celebrated almost everywhere.

media.author: Sami Mlouhi

questions.description: A dish with more nicknames than the class clown.
questions.question: You order Schupfnudeln with sauerkraut. Which name is NOT another name for them?
hints: The name you're looking for belongs to a different Swabian dish.
That other dish is stuffed pasta pockets.
The nickname comes from the story that people hid meat from God inside them during Lent.
questions.fun_fact: Schupfnudeln get their name from “schupfen”: rolling them back and forth between your hands.

questions.description: Noodles with so much cheese that it stretches like chewing gum.
questions.question: Which region do Käsespätzle with fried onions come from?
hints: The region is in the south of Germany.
People there are said to be especially thrifty.
Its center is Stuttgart.
questions.fun_fact: Traditionally, real Spätzle are scraped off a wooden board straight into boiling water.

media.author: Takeaway

questions.question: Semmelknödel are made from stale Semmeln. “Semmel” is to Munich as … is to Berlin?
hints: You're looking for the Berlin word for a bread roll.
The name probably comes from the slit cut into the top.
It starts with “Schr”.
questions.fun_fact: In Hamburg, a bread roll is traditionally called a “Rundstück”.

media.credit: Takeaway · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Takeaway

questions.description: A dumpling with a secret inside.
questions.question: You're invited for dinner, and they serve “Gefillde” with bacon sauce and sauerkraut. Whose home are you most likely in?
hints: In this region, potatoes come to the table in many forms.
Gefillde are stuffed potato dumplings.
Their state borders France and Luxembourg.
questions.fun_fact: The dumplings are usually stuffed with liverwurst and ground meat.

media.author: Hans Bernhard Schwerin

questions.description: Here even the air smells like dessert.
questions.question: I have spinning carousels and a Ferris wheel, and everywhere smells of gebrannte Mandeln (sugar-roasted almonds). What am I?
hints: I only come to town for a few days, then move on.
I have raffle booths and bumper cars.
In the Rhineland, people call me “Kirmes”.
questions.fun_fact: Gebrannte Mandeln are roasted with sugar in a copper kettle until the sugar caramelizes.

media.author: 4028mdk09

questions.question: This sour-milk cheese has a strong smell, almost no fat, and is often sold as a “Roller.” Which mountain range is it named after?
hints: The range is in the middle of Germany.
The Brocken is there.
Witches are said to dance there on Walpurgis Night.
questions.fun_fact: Harzer cheese usually has less than one percent fat, but a lot of protein.

media.author: Kimberly Vardeman

People in Austria also know the bake by this name.
The bread slices are stacked in it like logs of firewood.
questions.fun_fact: Ofenschlupfer is a classic way to use up leftovers: it turns stale bread rolls or Hefezopf (braided sweet bread) into dessert.

media.author: Unknown authorUnknown author

questions.description: From the bag into the pot, and Grandma supposedly never notices.
questions.question: Pfanni was founded in Munich in 1949. What are most Pfanni products made from?
hints: It grows underground.
People make dumplings and mash from it.
It once came to Europe from South America.
questions.fun_fact: Pfanni belongs to Unilever today and is made in Stavenhagen, in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

hints: I often end up in German school bags.
People love to dunk me in a glass of milk.
My name joins a king's son with my shape.
questions.fun_fact: Prinzenrolle is sold under the De Beukelaer brand, founded in 1869 in Antwerp, Belgium.

Butter lies between thin layers of dough.

You take it from the finished dough before baking.
It is alive and must be fed with flour and water so you can start the next dough.
questions.fun_fact: Some bakeries have looked after their Anstellgut for decades and keep baking with it again and again.

The end of the line rhymes with “Schmalz.”

The fairground is in the Bad Cannstatt district.

The angled skis push snow in front of them and hold you back.

The art movement is named after the Latin word for “expression.”

questions.description: A big-city adventure where the grown-ups are just extras.
questions.question: Emil Tischbein's money is stolen on the train. With Gustav and lots of other kids, he chases the thief through which city?
hints: Emil is actually on his way to visit his grandmother.
Emil travels from a small town to a huge city.
Today it is Germany's capital.
questions.fun_fact: “Emil and the Detectives” came out in 1929, and the first film of it followed as early as 1931.

questions.description: A film where even the houses look like they had a bad night's sleep.
questions.question: The silent film “The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari” is famous for its crooked, painted sets. In which year did it reach theaters?
hints: Germany was a young republic at the time.
Movie theaters didn't have sound films yet.
The First World War had ended only a little over a year before.
questions.fun_fact: Some of the slanted shadows and lights in “Caligari” were simply painted onto the sets.

questions.description: A chancellor who barely had time to hang up his name plate.
questions.question: This general was Reich Chancellor from December 1932 to January 1933, the last one before Hitler. Who is he?
hints: Before that, he was Minister of the Reichswehr (the army).
He was in office for barely two months.
His surname comes from the German verb for sneaking up quietly.
questions.fun_fact: Schleicher wanted to bring together trade unions and part of the Nazi Party, an idea called the “Querfront” (cross-front).

questions.description: An engine that squeezes air until it gets too hot to handle.
questions.question: About what percentage of the energy in its fuel did Rudolf Diesel's first working engine use in 1897?
hints: Most of the energy was lost as heat.
The steam engines of his time managed only about 10 percent.
It was roughly a quarter.
questions.fun_fact: Diesel's first test engine nearly exploded in 1893: a pressure gauge flew just past his head.

media.author: Henri Aja

questions.description: From a village near Hildesheim to Troy is farther than any GPS thinks.
questions.question: This actress from Lower Saxony played the beautiful Helen in “Troy”. Who is she?
hints: She first worked as a model in Paris.
For Fatih Akin's “In the Fade” she won Best Actress at Cannes in 2017.
In “Inglourious Basterds” she played the actress Bridget von Hammersmark.
questions.fun_fact: She was born Diane Heidkrüger in Algermissen, near Hildesheim.

media.author: Martin Kraft

questions.description: The rarest acceptance speech in German TV history: “No, thank you.”
questions.question: Which literary critic was to receive the German Television Award for lifetime achievement in 2008 and turned it down on stage?
hints: He was born in Poland.
He was nicknamed the “Pope of Literature”.
He hosted “Das Literarische Quartett” on ZDF.
questions.fun_fact: Afterwards, Thomas Gottschalk had a separate talk with him about television, which ZDF aired shortly after.

media.author: Eli Francis elifrancis

questions.description: Detective by day, microphone in hand by night: free time is overrated.
questions.question: This actress from the Weimar “Tatort” also sings in a band. Which one?
hints: She first became known as an MTV host.
The band is a trio: her and two men.
The band's name is a capital city on the Vltava river.
questions.fun_fact: Nora Tschirner became famous in cinemas alongside Til Schweiger in “Keinohrhasen”.

media.author: Manfred Werner (Tsui)

questions.description: A birthday party for a whole country, only with flags in place of candles.
questions.question: Every year on “Tag der Republik,” East Germany celebrated its founding with parades in East Berlin. What was the date?
hints: The day fell in the fall.
In 1989 it was celebrated for the 40th time, about a month before the Berlin Wall fell.
The date is four days after today’s Day of German Unity.
questions.fun_fact: For the 40th anniversary in 1989, Mikhail Gorbachev came to East Berlin, and just one month later the Wall fell.

media.credit: Deutsche Post der DDR · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Deutsche Post der DDR

questions.description: Alexanderplatz is where tourists, pigeons and a good helping of East Berlin nostalgia all meet.
questions.question: You're standing on Alexanderplatz in Berlin. What rises 368 m (1,207 ft) into the sky there, topped by a silver sphere?
hints: It is the tallest structure in Germany.
Inside the sphere there is a restaurant that slowly turns.
From here, pictures were broadcast to the television sets of East Germany.
questions.fun_fact: When the sun shines on the sphere, a bright cross appears on it, and Berliners called this “the Pope's revenge.”

media.credit: Martin Falbisoner · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Martin Falbisoner

questions.description: The day when Bollerwagen cover more miles than in the whole rest of the year.
questions.question: On Men's Day, often called “Herrentag” in East Germany, men head out pulling Bollerwagen (wooden handcarts). Which holiday does it fall on?
hints: It is always on a Thursday.
It comes 39 days after Easter Sunday.
The holiday remembers Jesus going up into heaven.
questions.fun_fact: In East Germany, Ascension Day stopped being a public holiday in 1967, but many people celebrated Herrentag anyway.

media.author: rs-foto

questions.description: For many East German kids, their first vocabulary words looked like a secret code.
questions.question: From 5th grade on, East German kids had to learn Russian. Which script is Russian text like in the photo written in?
hints: It is named after a saint.
Bulgarian, Serbian and Ukrainian use it too.
It is named after a monk who lived in the 9th century with his brother Methodius.
questions.fun_fact: Anyone who can read Cyrillic knows that the Russian “PECTOPAH” simply means “restaurant”.

questions.description: People's property had an expiry date; it just wasn't printed on the package.
questions.question: You find an old radio made by “VEB Stern-Radio Berlin”. In what year did such East German companies stop being VEBs?
hints: A law passed by East Germany's parliament, the Volkskammer, turned them into corporations.
In the same year, the Deutsche Mark arrived in the East.
It is the year of German reunification.
questions.fun_fact: From 1990, the Treuhandanstalt agency was tasked with privatizing more than 8,000 state-owned companies.

media.credit: Thomas Quine · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Thomas Quine

questions.description: A constitution from the other side that later got a thorough makeover.
questions.question: What was NOT in East Germany's first constitution of 1949?
questions.answer: The leading role of the SED
hints: The 1949 constitution was meant to look democratic and was modeled on the Weimar constitution.
The missing point was only added with the new constitution of 1968.
It's about the party that called the shots anyway.
questions.fun_fact: On paper, the 1949 constitution even guaranteed every citizen the right to emigrate.

media.author: Wilhelm II.,  König von Preußen

questions.description: The art of renaming a workers' strike until it fits the party handbook.
questions.question: Strike leaders were put on trial, and East German schoolbooks gave June 17, 1953, a name. What was it?
hints: The term shows the party's official view, not the strikers' view.
The SED wanted to deny that workers had risen up against their own workers' state.
A word from before 1945, plus a failed seizure of power.
questions.fun_fact: Bertolt Brecht mocked it at the time in a poem, saying the government should simply elect another people.

media.author: U. A. Saarinen

questions.description: A summer festival that suddenly made East Berlin very colorful.
questions.question: At the 1973 World Festival of Youth and Students in East Berlin, the US civil rights activist in the photo was celebrated like a star. Who is she?
hints: She was a philosopher and an open communist.
Her trial in the US was a big topic in East German schools in the early 1970s.
Her big Afro hairstyle became the symbol of a whole movement.
questions.fun_fact: East German children sent her huge numbers of rose postcards in prison, in a campaign called “A Million Roses for Angela.”

media.credit: Koard, Peter · CC BY-SA 3.0 de · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Koard, Peter

questions.description: Wide sidewalks, tiled palaces and a street sign that didn't last long.
questions.question: In 1961, East Berlin's grand boulevard Stalinallee got a new name. What is its stretch of wedding-cake-style buildings called to this day?
hints: After Stalin's death, his name was no longer welcome, even in the GDR.
The new name honored a thinker whose ideas the SED claimed to follow.
He wrote “The Communist Manifesto” together with Friedrich Engels.
questions.fun_fact: The eastern part of the old Stalinallee is now called Frankfurter Allee.

media.credit: Michielverbeek · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Michielverbeek

questions.description: A building in East Berlin whose door sign took longer to negotiate than most house rules.
questions.question: The “Ständige Vertretung” (Permanent Mission) on Hannoversche Straße in East Berlin opened in 1974, first led by Günter Gaus. What was it?
questions.answer: Bonn's stand-in for an embassy in East Germany
wrong_answers: The seat of East Berlin's mayor
The United Nations office in East Germany
The meeting place of East Germany's parliament
hints: It came about after the Basic Treaty of 1972.
West Germany didn't want to recognize East Germany as a foreign country.
Its head was practically an ambassador, but wasn't allowed to be called one.
questions.fun_fact: Today, the Berlin pub “Ständige Vertretung” recalls the Bonn years by serving Kölsch beer.

media.credit: Gerd Danigel · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Gerd Danigel

questions.description: She decided what was learned in East German classrooms, and for quite a long time.
questions.question: Who was East Germany's Minister of Education from 1963 to 1989?
hints: Because of the tint of her hair, people called her the “purple witch” (lila Hexe).
After reunification she lived in Chile until her death.
Her husband led East Germany from 1971 to 1989.
questions.fun_fact: Margot Honecker died in Santiago, Chile, in 2016.

media.credit: Dejan Krsmanovic · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Dejan Krsmanovic

questions.description: The very first paper of your life, and you didn't even sign it yourself.
questions.question: The Standesamt (registry office) issues this document shortly after birth. It lists your name, place of birth and parents. What is it?
hints: You need it later, for example when you want to get married.
It puts one very specific day on paper.
It officially records when and where you came into the world.
questions.fun_fact: In Germany, a birth must be reported to the Standesamt within one week.

media.credit: sergio santos · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: sergio santos

questions.description: A roommate who never pays rent but still takes over every corner.
questions.question: It grows in damp corners when rooms aren't aired out enough, is often black or green, and likes old bread too. What is it?
hints: Regular Stoßlüften (opening the windows wide for a few minutes) helps against it.
You often find it behind wardrobes or in the bathroom.
It is a fungus and forms a fuzzy layer on forgotten food.
questions.fun_fact: In German, “Schimmel” is also the word for a white horse.

media.credit: Doggo19292 · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Doggo19292

questions.description: German homes follow a breathing routine stricter than any gym.
questions.question: For Stoßlüften, you open the windows wide for a few minutes instead of leaving them tilted open for a long time. Why?
questions.answer: So damp air gets out but the walls stay warm
wrong_answers: So the dust blows off furniture and shelves
So no insects fly into the home
hints: It's about the air and the heating.
It has to do with cooking, showering and breathing indoors.
It's meant to stop mold while still saving heating energy.
questions.fun_fact: In winter, experts recommend doing Stoßlüften several times a day for about five to ten minutes.

media.author: Karl432

questions.description: All the neighbors meet here, but nobody stays a second longer than they have to.
questions.question: In an apartment building, it leads from the front door to the apartments. The mailboxes often hang here, and the light goes off after a few minutes. What is it?
hints: Every resident walks through it every day.
Sometimes shoes or a stroller stand here.
You pass through it before unlocking your own apartment door.
questions.fun_fact: The switch that turns off the hallway light by itself has its own long German name: Treppenlichtautomat.

media.credit: ChristianSchd · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: ChristianSchd

questions.description: The tiniest VIP on your key ring: looks worthless, but sometimes nothing works without it.
questions.question: Lots of people keep a small plastic token like this on their key ring. What is it for?
hints: You get it back afterwards.
You push it into a small lock.
Then you can push something with wheels away.
questions.fun_fact: Most of these locks also take a 1-euro coin instead of a token.

media.credit: M. Findlay · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: M. Findlay

questions.description: Units are like street names: everyone uses them, nobody asks who's behind them.
questions.question: On your charger and your weather app you meet units named after scientists. Which one is NOT named after a German?
hints: Three of the scientists spoke German, one spoke Italian.
Fahrenheit came from Danzig, even though Americans use his scale the most today.
You're looking for the inventor of the first battery.
questions.fun_fact: For the zero point of his scale, Fahrenheit used the lowest temperature he could reach with a mix of ice, water and ammonium chloride.

media.author: Huwanglaimtangms

questions.description: A TV show you won't find in the dairy aisle, even though its name sounds like it belongs there.
questions.question: For years, Ranga Yogeshwar explained science on WDR in the show “Quarks & …”. How does the title end?
hints: The show started on WDR in 1993.
You often see it in company names, too.
It's short for “Compagnie”, or company.
questions.fun_fact: Ranga Yogeshwar was born in Luxembourg and studied physics in Aachen.

media.credit: J.N. Eskra · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: J.N. Eskra

questions.description: A company from Mainz that got famous in 2020 faster than any Fastnacht band.
questions.question: Uğur Şahin and Özlem Türeci researched cancer treatments at their Mainz company BioNTech. What made it world-famous with Pfizer in late 2020?
hints: It has to do with the pandemic.
It is based on a technique called mRNA.
You got it as a shot in the upper arm.
questions.fun_fact: Şahin and Türeci are a married couple, and they are said to have gone straight back to the lab after their wedding.

media.author: Flocci Nivis

questions.description: A story that shines so brightly you can hardly see the holes in it.
questions.question: An emigrant mechanic is said to have built light bulbs like this one in New York before Edison. Which town near Hanover was he from?
hints: His name was Heinrich Göbel.
The town lies at the foot of the Deister hills.
Its name sounds like the German command “jump!”.
questions.fun_fact: No proof of Göbel's invention was ever found: the story mostly came up in patent fights against Edison around 1893.

media.author: Pfnicholls

questions.description: A mountain with a family: his wife and kids stand right next door, all made of stone.
questions.question: The Watzmann is the highest peak in Berchtesgaden National Park. About how high is it?
hints: The Zugspitze is higher, at 2,962 meters (9,718 ft).
It is said to be the highest mountain that lies entirely on German soil.
The number is just over 2,700.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says the Watzmann was a cruel king who was turned to stone along with his wife and children.

media.author: Jörg Braukmann

questions.description: A rock that distracts boatmen more than a phone distracts drivers.
questions.question: Heinrich Heine's Lorelei poem begins: “I don't know what it means that I am so …” Which word is missing?
hints: Next, the speaker can't get “a fairy tale from ancient times” out of his mind.
The boatman hears the Lorelei's song, forgets the reef and goes down.
It's the opposite of merry.
questions.fun_fact: The well-known tune for Heine's poem is by Friedrich Silcher and was published in 1837.

media.author: Jörg Braukmann

questions.question: About 150 million years ago, the Swabian Alb was the sea floor, and today it is full of caves. What rock is it mostly made of?
hints: You can find fossil ammonites and shells in it.
Rainwater slowly dissolves this rock, and that's how caves form.
Chalk and marble are close relatives of it.
questions.fun_fact: Caves in the Swabian Alb held the oldest known musical instruments in the world: flutes made of bone and ivory, about 40,000 years old.

It is also home to northern Germany's highest mountain.
A steam train runs up the Brocken.
questions.fun_fact: By 2006, about two dozen lynxes had been released in the Harz, and today their descendants roam as far as Hesse and Thuringia.

questions.question: The Middle Rhine Valley is to clifftop fortresses as the Münsterland is to…?
hints: There are hardly any hills in the Münsterland.
Instead of cliffs, people there protected themselves with wide ditches.
Burg Vischering and Burg Hülshoff are famous examples.
questions.fun_fact: The poet Annette von Droste-Hülshoff was born at Burg Hülshoff in the Münsterland in 1797.

questions.description: The ground here is only sleeping, and sometimes it even bubbles in its sleep.
questions.question: How long ago did a volcano last erupt in the Eifel?
hints: No history book tells of it.
It was at the end of the last Ice Age.
People already lived in Europe then, but there were no farmers yet.
questions.fun_fact: The Ulmener Maar is thought to be the Eifel's youngest volcano, and today it is a small, round lake.

media.author: NoahSchmitzFotografie

questions.description: A left foot like a hammer and a good mood like at Carnival.
questions.question: I was born in Poland, had a rocket of a left foot, and I'm still the darling of Cologne's fans. My nickname is a short form of my last name. Who am I?
hints: In 2014 I became world champion with Germany.
The club closest to my heart is 1. FC Köln.
Everyone just calls me “Poldi”.
questions.fun_fact: Besides soccer, Podolski runs his own döner kebab chain called “Mangal Döner”.

media.author: Martin Falbisoner

questions.description: It invites itself to every coffee-and-cake afternoon in the garden.
questions.question: It has yellow and black stripes, comes for the plum cake in late summer and stings if you swat at it. Which animal group does it belong to?
hints: It has six legs.
Bees and ants belong to this group too.
The group's name begins with “In…”.
questions.fun_fact: Only female wasps have a stinger – the males can't sting at all.

media.author: Silar

questions.description: Buzzes like a mini helicopter and loves to rent a room from a mouse.
questions.question: In the garden you find a bumblebee nest in an old mouse hole. About how many bumblebees live in it?
hints: A bumblebee colony is much smaller than a honeybee colony.
A honeybee colony has tens of thousands of bees in summer.
It's more than 100 but fewer than 1,000.
questions.fun_fact: Bumblebees warm up by shivering their flight muscles, so they can fly on cool spring days when honeybees stay in the hive.

media.author: Alvesgaspar

questions.description: A gardener with no hands, no feet and no garden shears.
questions.question: It's long and pink, has no legs, loosens the garden soil and crawls out of the ground after a rain shower. What is it?
hints: It lives under the ground in the garden.
Blackbirds love to pull it out of the lawn.
Its name tells you where it lives: in the soil.
questions.fun_fact: Earthworms have no eyes, but they can sense light through their skin.

media.credit: Shixart1985 · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Shixart1985

questions.description: It wears antlers, but you'll never hear it roar in the fall.
questions.question: This beetle lives only a few weeks as an adult. How long did it spend before that as a larva in rotting wood?
hints: The larva eats its way very slowly through old, rotting oak wood.
Its time as a larva is much longer than its life as a beetle.
This time is counted in years, but not in decades.
questions.fun_fact: The stag beetle is the largest beetle in Germany, and only the males have the antler-like jaws.

media.credit: Leonora Enking · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Leonora Enking

questions.description: A beachgoer with no swimsuit, but a season pass to the mudflats.
questions.question: You meet this animal on the mudflats of the North Sea. Which animal group does it belong to?
hints: It has a hard shell and two claws.
Lobsters and shrimp belong to this group too.
The zodiac sign Cancer is drawn as one of these animals.
questions.fun_fact: If a shore crab loses a claw, it grows back over its next few molts.

media.credit: John Haslam · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: John Haslam

questions.description: It wears a tie every day and still has never had an office job.
questions.question: It has a black head with white cheeks, a yellow chest and calls “zee-zee-bah”. Where does it prefer to build its nest?
questions.answer: In tree holes or nest boxes
wrong_answers: On the ground in tall grass
In the reeds by a lake
As a mud nest under the eaves
hints: It's a common garden bird from the tit family.
It stays all year round and likes to visit bird feeders in winter.
Many people hang wooden boxes with a small entrance hole in their gardens for it.
questions.fun_fact: A pair of great tits flies to its chicks with caterpillars several hundred times a day.

media.credit: Francis C. Franklin · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Francis C. Franklin

questions.description: A free garden concert: no entry fee, no tickets, and still sold out every day.
questions.question: Listen: which bird is singing here in the garden?
hints: It often sings at dawn from rooftops and TV antennas.
It likes to hop across the lawn and pull out worms.
The male is black and has a yellow-orange beak.
questions.fun_fact: Only the male blackbird is black – the female is brown.

media.author: Marie-Lan Taÿ Pamart

questions.description: A sausage on four legs that you must never put on the grill.
questions.question: It has short legs and a long body, and it was once meant to crawl into badger dens. What kind of animal is a Dackel?
hints: It comes from Germany and is also called a Teckel.
It is one of the most popular pets in Germany.
It barks when the doorbell rings.
questions.fun_fact: A colorful Dackel named “Waldi” was the mascot of the 1972 Olympic Games in Munich.

questions.description: A high-rise with no elevator, but with very hard-working residents.
questions.question: You'll find big mounds of needles and twigs like this one in German forests. Which animals built it?

They can spray acid to defend themselves.
They crawl on six legs and drag needles into their nest.
questions.fun_fact: Red wood ants are protected by law in Germany, so you're not allowed to destroy their mounds.
