media.author: Claire Pegrum

questions.description: Some nicknames sound a lot scarier than the people who wear them.
questions.question: Which German musician goes by the nickname “Panikrocker”?
hints: He comes from Gronau in Westphalia.
He has lived for decades in Hamburg's Hotel Atlantic.
He almost always wears a hat and sunglasses, and he sang “Sonderzug nach Pankow”.
questions.fun_fact: Before he became famous, Udo Lindenberg played drums, including in Klaus Doldinger's band Passport.

media.author: Shixart1985

questions.description: Modesty is a virtue, but this band gets along just fine without it.
questions.question: Which Berlin band, founded in 1982, calls itself, tongue in cheek, “the best band in the world”?

One hit asks: “Junge, warum hast du nichts gelernt?”
Its members are Farin Urlaub, Bela B. and Rodrigo González.
questions.fun_fact: The band split up in 1988 and got back together in 1993.

media.author: Tyler Savitski

questions.description: Three letters, two musicians and quite a lot of synthesizer.
questions.question: The electro duo D.A.F., with Gabi Delgado and Robert Görl, sang “Der Räuber und der Prinz” in 1981. What does D.A.F. stand for?

The “F” stands for something you share between friends.
The second word refers to the country of the Statue of Liberty.
questions.fun_fact: D.A.F. is seen as a pioneer of Electronic Body Music, or EBM for short.

It has a side we never get to see from Earth.

I share my name with a scientist who pointed a telescope at Jupiter in 1610.

media.author: NJM2010

At the end of each round, a mask comes off.

questions.fun_fact: The three black lions on gold in the state's greater coat of arms are the old arms of the Staufer family.

hints: They live on a farm.

They oink and have a curly tail.
questions.fun_fact: German hunters have their own words for wild boars: the male is a “Keiler” and the mother a “Bache”.

media.author: Tilman2007

questions.description: This animal has been leaping on a coat of arms for centuries and still hasn't landed.

hints: I have hooves.

questions.fun_fact: A white horse leaps on the coat of arms of North Rhine-Westphalia too: the Westfalenross.

hints: Locals use the same word, as a verb, for the grilling itself.
The meat on it is usually marinated pork neck steak.
The word comes from swinging the grill grate back and forth.
questions.fun_fact: In Saarland, even the meat on the grill is often just called a “Schwenker”.

hints: You say it after a stroke of luck, not before.
The animal in the saying is a popular gift on New Year's Eve.
The animal oinks.
questions.fun_fact: One explanation: at old contests, the last-place finisher often got a piglet as a consolation prize, so they had “had pig”.

media.author: Cygnus921

questions.description: Grandma's pharmacy was usually in the vegetable drawer.
questions.question: With honey it becomes cough syrup; warmed in a small bag on the ear, it's said to ease earache. Which vegetable is it?
hints: It's almost always in the kitchen.

Cutting it often makes your eyes water.
questions.fun_fact: When you cut an onion, it releases a substance that rises into the air and makes your eyes water.

media.author: Fæ

In the 2003 final, it beat the Kölner Haie.
Its mascot wears a tailcoat and can't fly.
questions.fun_fact: Krefeld was once so famous for its silk fabrics that it is still called the “City of Velvet and Silk” today.

media.author: Jab18071

It's roughly a quarter of a day.

media.author: Ben Harris

questions.description: Swimsuit on, picnic basket packed: now you just need the right S-Bahn train.
questions.question: An old German hit song goes “Pack die Badehose ein … und dann nischt wie raus nach Wannsee”. In which city is the Wannsee?
hints: Young Conny Froboess sang the song in 1951.

It is the capital of Germany.
questions.fun_fact: Strandbad Wannsee, the lake's big public beach, opened in 1907 and is one of the largest inland lake beaches in Europe.

questions.description: A river that sets off in Austria and makes its career in Swabia.

The town of Landsberg carries the river's name as part of its own.
questions.fun_fact: Augsburg lies west of the Lech, so it belongs to Swabia, not to Old Bavaria.

It holds the sand on the beach

High waves and storm surges can't get over it.
questions.fun_fact: Sheep on the dike keep the grass short and press the soil firm with their hooves.

media.author: Txllxt TxllxT

wrong_answers: So they float on top of the water
So the sand lasts for more bags
So they dry out faster afterward
hints: A bag stuffed full is as hard as a rock.
Gaps stay open between hard, round bags.
A bag that isn't quite full can be pressed flat and shaped.
questions.fun_fact: A filled sandbag weighs about 15 kg (33 lb), and a long wall needs thousands of them.

media.author: Andrea Booher

questions.description: Golden treasures you can find without a treasure map.

hints: The pieces are so light that the waves easily wash them ashore.
Long ago, traders carried them on long journeys all the way to Rome.
Rügen and Usedom lie in it.
questions.fun_fact: Amber isn't a stone at all: it's tree resin that hardened over millions of years.

media.author: Manukyan Andranik

questions.description: A raindrop on a long journey, without any luggage.

hints: The Danube flows east.
It passes through ten countries.
Its delta is in Romania.
questions.fun_fact: On its way, the Danube flows through four capital cities: Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest and Belgrade.

Whatever it can't digest comes out the back end.

The name contains the German word for the muddy seabed.

questions.question: Here, people are clinking glasses. According to superstition, which drink should you never toast with?
hints: It's the simplest drink of all.
Sailors in particular found it spooky.
It comes straight out of the tap.
questions.fun_fact: An old sailors' superstition says that toasting with water brings bad luck at sea.

media.credit: Smuzcafe · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Smuzcafe

questions.description: Great in the sauce, bad for a first kiss, and for certain creatures of the night.
questions.question: According to folk belief, who does a bulb of garlic hung over the door keep away?
hints: These creatures are out and about at night.
They sleep in a coffin during the day.
Count Dracula is the most famous of them.
questions.fun_fact: Garlic has been used as a medicinal plant for thousands of years, for example in ancient Egypt.

media.credit: Luis Miguel Bugallo Sánchez (Lmbuga) · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Luis Miguel Bugallo Sánchez (Lmbuga)

questions.description: A shrub people turn into syrup, tea and a whole lot of folk belief.
questions.question: You want to make elderflower syrup and need the white blossoms. In which month does elder usually bloom in Germany?
hints: It's already warm.
Strawberries are ripe at the same time.
The longest day of the year falls in this month.
questions.fun_fact: People used to say a good spirit lived in the elder, so you should take off your hat in front of the shrub.

media.credit: Gerwin Sturm from Vienna, Austria · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Gerwin Sturm from Vienna, Austria

questions.description: When even ghosts show up to work on time.
questions.question: In German folk belief, the Geisterstunde (“ghost hour”) begins at midnight. At what time does it end?
hints: The name already tells you how long it lasts.
It lasts exactly 60 minutes.
The tower clock then strikes only a single time.
questions.fun_fact: In many legends, ghosts must vanish by the first crow of the rooster at the latest.

media.credit: Jorge Royan · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jorge Royan

questions.description: A month with more moods than a cat in front of an empty bowl.
questions.question: Sun in the morning, hail at noon, rain in the evening: which month do Germans say “does whatever it wants”?
hints: It's in spring.
Easter often falls in this month.
On its first day, you're allowed to play tricks on people.
questions.fun_fact: In spring, warm and cold air masses often clash, which is why the weather changes so fast then.

media.credit: Antoine Chintreuil · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Antoine Chintreuil

questions.description: Dice, lottery, card games: some people just always win.
questions.question: You win at dice three times in a row. What do Germans call you then?
hints: The word praises you for chance, not for skill.
You get called this too when you find a coin on the street.
A red-and-white fly agaric mushroom is a lucky symbol.
questions.fun_fact: In Germany the poisonous fly agaric mushroom is a popular good-luck charm, for example on New Year's Eve cards.

media.credit: Toshiyuki IMAI from Kyoto, Japan · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Toshiyuki IMAI from Kyoto, Japan

questions.description: Shoes you should never wear on the sidewalk.
questions.question: Look at the photo: how many blades does this pair of ice skates have in total?
hints: Count the boots first.
Under each boot there is a metal blade.
One boot, one blade, and there are two boots.
questions.fun_fact: Thousands of years ago, people tied animal bones under their feet to glide across the ice.

media.credit: Mudflattop · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Mudflattop

questions.description: Here people leave the mountain faster than kids leave the classroom before vacation.
questions.question: On the Kandahar run in Garmisch-Partenkirchen, ski racers speed down at over 100 km/h (60 mph). What is the fastest event in alpine skiing?
hints: It has only a few gates.
Its course is the longest in alpine skiing.
Its English name simply describes heading down the mountain.
questions.fun_fact: In a World Cup race in Wengen, a skier was once clocked at almost 162 km/h (about 100 mph).

media.credit: Fotofloh · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Fotofloh

questions.description: The widest path in the world, and nobody ever walks on it.
questions.question: You ski down it from the top of the mountain. Easy ones are marked blue, medium ones red and hard ones black. What is it?
hints: Every ski resort has them.
The lift takes you up, and then you go back down on it.
In German it's called “Piste,” a word borrowed from French.
questions.fun_fact: The German and British word “piste” comes from French and first meant “track” or “trail.”

media.credit: Marco Bonomo · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Marco Bonomo

questions.description: First a cozy lie-down, then things get serious, a bit like Sunday morning.
questions.question: In the biathlon sprint, athletes shoot twice. The first time, they lie on their stomachs. How do they shoot the second time?
hints: The second position is harder than the first.
The rifle doesn't rest on the ground.
The athletes simply stay upright on their skis.
questions.fun_fact: In prone shooting the target is only 4.5 cm (1.8 in) wide; in standing shooting it's 11.5 cm (4.5 in).

media.credit: Steffen Prößdorf · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Steffen Prößdorf

questions.description: Four gold medals in one suitcase: that's excess baggage on the flight home.
questions.question: In 2017, Johannes Rydzek from Oberstdorf became the first Nordic combined athlete to win four golds at one World Championships. Where?
hints: The place is in northern Europe.
No other place has hosted the Nordic World Ski Championships as often.
Its name has five letters and starts with L.
questions.fun_fact: At the 2018 Olympics, Rydzek, Fabian Rießle and Eric Frenzel took a German one-two-three in the large hill individual event.

media.credit: Sandro Halank, Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Sandro Halank, Wikimedia Commons

questions.description: Two letters that tell you how much courage to bring along.
questions.question: At the Four Hills Tournament you hear “hill HS 142.” Which measure replaced the old K-point as the hill's official rating?
hints: The measure describes the whole hill, not just one point on the slope.
It is measured from the takeoff table to the end of the landing area.
It tells you how big the hill is, in two words.
questions.fun_fact: The K in K-point first stood for “kritischer Punkt” (critical point); today it officially means “Konstruktionspunkt” (construction point).

media.credit: Arne Müseler · CC BY-SA 3.0 de · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Arne Müseler

questions.description: Ski school in the morning, Germknödel at lunch, waiting in line for the lift all afternoon: the perfect ski day.
questions.question: I don't make a single turn. Both ski tips point straight down the valley, and I keep getting faster. What am I called?
hints: Braking is not part of me.
The path goes straight down the fall line.
My name is the German word for a shot.
questions.fun_fact: During a schuss, downhill racers crouch into a tuck so the wind slows them down less.

media.credit: DimiTalen · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: DimiTalen

questions.description: A hut where the walk to the snack stand is rather steep.
questions.question: The Münchner Haus is Germany's highest mountain hut, at almost 3,000 m (9,800 ft). On which mountain does it stand?
hints: The mountain is in Bavaria.
The border with Austria runs over its summit.
A golden cross stands on its summit, and it is near Garmisch-Partenkirchen.
questions.fun_fact: Right next to the Münchner Haus, a weather station of the German Weather Service measures wind and snow.

media.credit: Cactus26 · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Cactus26

questions.description: An artwork you have to water instead of dust.
questions.question: In Kassel, basalt stones like these stand next to trees, part of an artwork that began in 1982. Who came up with it?
hints: The artwork started at the documenta art show.
Every tree planted comes with a stone.
The artist almost always wore a felt hat.
questions.fun_fact: The last of the 7,000 trees was planted in 1987 by Beuys's son, a year after the artist died.

media.credit: Dvdgmz · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Dvdgmz

questions.description: Columns, columns, columns: the ancient world had a big fan in Prussia.
questions.question: You're standing in Berlin's Lustgarten in front of the Altes Museum with its 18 columns. Who designed this building?
hints: He was Prussia's most famous architect of the 19th century.
He also designed the Schauspielhaus on the Gendarmenmarkt.
His last name sounds almost like the German word for ham.
questions.fun_fact: The Altes Museum opened in 1830 and was Berlin's first public museum.

media.credit: Bahnfrend · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bahnfrend

questions.description: A chair that needed a world stage before anyone was allowed to sit on it.
questions.question: Ludwig Mies van der Rohe designed this chair in 1929. What is it called?
hints: Seen from the side, its steel frame crosses in an X.
It stood in the German pavilion at a world's fair.
The city lies on the Mediterranean and has the Sagrada Família.
questions.fun_fact: Mies van der Rohe was the last director of the Bauhaus, from 1930 to 1933.

media.credit: Wasily at Dutch Wikipedia · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Wasily at Dutch Wikipedia

questions.description: Sunday morning, pajama pants under your jacket, and off to the bakery.
questions.question: You're fetching Brötchen on Sunday. Which word is NOT a regional name for a bread roll?
hints: Three of the words are used for bread rolls in Berlin, Bavaria and Swabia.
The word you're looking for also comes from Berlin.
It means a slice of bread with something on it, like a school snack.
questions.fun_fact: In Hamburg, a bread roll is called a “Rundstück”, and in Saarland a “Weck”.

media.credit: Wilfredor · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Wilfredor

questions.description: A pocket you're allowed to bite into without getting in trouble.
questions.question: For an Apfeltasche, you put apple filling on puff pastry, fold it over and press the edges with a fork. Why?
questions.answer: So the filling doesn't leak out
hints: It's about the edge, not the middle.
In the oven, the filling gets hot and runny.
Without a sealed edge, you end up with apple stuck to the baking sheet.
questions.fun_fact: Steam builds up inside while it bakes, so people often cut a few small slits in the top.

media.credit: Evan-Amos · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Evan-Amos

questions.description: Here, every calorie is carefully decorated with whipped cream.
questions.question: It sells cream cakes and chocolates, often has a small café, and its master was once called a “Zuckerbäcker” (sugar baker). What is the shop called?
hints: Bread and rolls aren't the main thing here.
The job there is a trade of its own, with its own master's exam.
The master here is the Konditor.
questions.fun_fact: The word “Konditor” comes from the Latin “condire”, meaning “to preserve” or “to season”.

media.credit: Andy Li · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Andy Li

questions.description: A Christmas song that always leaves the kitchen looking like a snowstorm hit it.
questions.question: In the song “In der Weihnachtsbäckerei”, many a “Knilch” makes a huge mess. Between which two ingredients?
hints: The song is by Rolf Zuckowski.
In the German line, one of the ingredients rhymes with “Knilch”.
One is a white powder, the other comes from the cow.
questions.fun_fact: Rolf Zuckowski released “In der Weihnachtsbäckerei” in 1987, and today it is one of the best-known German Christmas songs.

media.credit: Ralph Daily from Birmingham, United States · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ralph Daily from Birmingham, United States

questions.description: Cookies that refuse to be eaten right away.
questions.question: Long ago, people cut cookies into stars and hearts, poked a hole in them before baking and threaded a ribbon through. What for?
questions.answer: As decorations for the Christmas tree
hints: The cookies were meant to be looked at for a while before being eaten.
They were hung up somewhere.
Today, mostly glass balls and tinsel hang there.
questions.fun_fact: Before glass ornaments existed, Germans decorated Christmas trees with apples, nuts and baked treats.

media.credit: ktk17028 · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: ktk17028

questions.description: A pastry that's hollow inside but still never shows off.
questions.question: What kind of dough is this pastry made from?
hints: The dough is cooked in a pot on the stove first.
In the oven, steam puffs it up into a hollow ball.
Eclairs and Spritzkuchen are made from it too.
questions.fun_fact: In German, calling someone a “Windbeutel” means they're a show-off: big on the outside, nothing but air inside.

media.credit: Tamorlan · CC BY-SA 2.5 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Tamorlan

questions.description: A trophy that makes arms shake in Berlin every year.
questions.question: You lift the DFB-Pokal high after the final in Berlin. Roughly how heavy is it?
hints: A single player can lift it easily.
It's much heavier than a full carton of milk.
It weighs about as much as six 1-liter cartons of milk.
questions.fun_fact: The DFB-Pokal is about 52 centimeters (20 in) tall and holds about eight liters (2 gallons).

media.credit: Tobi 87 · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Tobi 87

questions.description: Here every win is celebrated like an Äppelwoi festival on the Main.
questions.question: You're standing in the Frankfurt fan section. Which nickname for Eintracht will you NOT hear there?
hints: One real Frankfurt nickname comes from the animal on the club crest.
One of the names belongs to a club from the Lower Rhine.
It's Borussia Mönchengladbach's nickname.
questions.fun_fact: At Eintracht home games, a real golden eagle named Attila is often in the stadium.

media.credit: Norbert Nagel · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Norbert Nagel

questions.description: A city that waited so long for this night that its cheers had started gathering dust.
questions.question: You're celebrating Frankfurt's 2022 Europa League win in Seville. When had Eintracht last won a European trophy before that?
hints: Back then the competition was still called the UEFA Cup.
Their opponent in the final was Borussia Mönchengladbach.
It was more than 40 years earlier.
questions.fun_fact: In the 2022 final against Rangers, Kevin Trapp saved Aaron Ramsey's kick in the penalty shootout.

media.credit: Diliff · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Diliff

questions.description: A small piece of cardboard that can make grown men sulk.
questions.question: A player gets a yellow card in a match. How many yellow cards does he need in total before he is sent off?
hints: Then the referee shows two colors at once.
In Germany this card is called “Gelb-Rot” (yellow-red).
The very next yellow card is enough.
questions.fun_fact: The Bundesliga has only had the yellow-red card since the 1991/92 season.

media.credit: Laslovarga · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Laslovarga

questions.description: Three trophies, one team bus and a bus driver with a very wide grin.
questions.question: In 2013, Bayern Munich became the first German club to win the treble. In which year did they do it a second time?
hints: The Champions League final was played in Lisbon.
In the final, Bayern beat Paris Saint-Germain 1–0.
The coach at the time was Hansi Flick.
questions.fun_fact: In the 2019–20 Champions League season, Bayern won all eleven of their games – no team had done that before.

media.credit: Jakub Hałun · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jakub Hałun

questions.description: A word that gets yelled on the field much shorter than it's spelled.
questions.question: On a German soccer field, he's called “Schiri” for short. What is the full word?
hints: He carries a whistle.
He shows yellow and red cards.
The second half of the word, “Richter”, means “judge”.
questions.fun_fact: A Bundesliga referee runs about 11 kilometers (7 miles) per game.

media.credit: Kithira · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Kithira

questions.description: A match hyped about as much as “Dinner for One” on New Year's Eve.
questions.question: When “Der Klassiker” is on in the Bundesliga, which teams are playing each other?
hints: It's the clash of the two most successful clubs of recent decades.
This match often helps decide who becomes German champion.
One of the teams is from Munich.
questions.fun_fact: The name is modeled on Spain's “El Clásico” between Real Madrid and FC Barcelona.

media.credit: Krzysztof Popławski · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Krzysztof Popławski

questions.description: Soccer is played with the feet – not every arm seems to know that yet.
questions.question: A defender deliberately handles the ball inside his own penalty area. What does the referee give?
hints: The attacking team is very happy.
It becomes a duel: one shooter against the goalkeeper.
The ball is placed on a spot inside the box.
questions.fun_fact: In German a penalty is called “Elfmeter” (eleven-meter), because the spot is exactly 11 meters (12 yards) from the goal.

media.credit: Gareth Williams from Redhill, England · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Gareth Williams from Redhill, England

questions.description: Pay once and roam the whole republic for a month, as long as the trains play along.
questions.question: How many euros a month did the Deutschlandticket cost when it started in May 2023?
hints: It was much cheaper than most old monthly passes.
It cost a lot more than a movie ticket, but much less than many old monthly passes for local transit.
Many people named it after its price: the “…-euro ticket”.
questions.fun_fact: The Deutschlandticket is valid on all buses and local trains across Germany, but not on the ICE or IC.

media.credit: calflier001 · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: calflier001

questions.description: First jetting around the world, then settling down in a Berlin palace.
questions.question: I was foreign minister twice, moved into Schloss Bellevue as Federal President in 2017 and was re-elected in 2022. Who am I?
hints: I belong to the SPD.
In 2010, I donated a kidney to my wife.
My last name starts with the German word for “stone”.
questions.fun_fact: Frank-Walter Steinmeier comes from Brakelsiek near Detmold and is the son of a carpenter.

media.credit: Michael.F.H.Barth · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Michael.F.H.Barth

questions.description: In politics, “left” has nothing to do with your turn signal.
questions.question: Parties like Die Linke are called “left-wing”. Where does this label originally come from?
questions.answer: The seating in the French parliament
wrong_answers: The hand you use to mark your ballot
The left column on the ballot paper
Where the party offices are in Berlin
hints: The story doesn't begin in Germany.
It goes back to the Revolution of 1789.
It's about where the members took their seats.
questions.fun_fact: In the Bundestag, too, Die Linke sits furthest to the left as seen from the chair.

media.credit: Ank Kumar · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ank Kumar

questions.description: A politician whose social media feed is more menu than party manifesto.
questions.question: I became Minister-President of Bavaria in 2018 and CSU leader in 2019, and I love posting photos of döner and bratwurst online. Who am I?
hints: I come from Nuremberg in Franconia.
In 2021 I wanted to be the Union's candidate for Chancellor, but Armin Laschet got the job.
My first name is Markus.
questions.fun_fact: The CSU only runs in elections in Bavaria and forms a joint group with the CDU in the Bundestag.

media.credit: User:Mattes · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: User:Mattes

questions.description: Suddenly there's a fat package of money, and everyone wonders who gets to unwrap it.
questions.question: Shortly after Russia attacked Ukraine in 2022, Olaf Scholz announced an extra 100 billion euros. Who got the money?
hints: Scholz announced it on a Sunday, in a special session of the Bundestag.
For years, many had complained that the equipment there was old or broken.
This means Germany's soldiers.
questions.fun_fact: The money is officially called a “Sondervermögen” (special fund), even though it is really debt.

media.credit: Daniel Schwen · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Daniel Schwen

questions.description: Ten fingers, one shape, and suddenly it's an election poster.
questions.question: Who made this way of holding the hands famous as a trademark?
hints: This person led Germany for a very long time.
This person grew up in East Germany.
She was the first woman to become chancellor.
questions.fun_fact: In 2013 a giant CDU poster in Berlin showed just these hands, made up of many small photos.

media.credit: Armin Linnartz · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Armin Linnartz

questions.description: Two friends, one signpost and a pretty big detour.
questions.question: Little Bear and Little Tiger go looking for the land of their dreams. Finish Janosch's book title: “Oh, wie schön ist …”
hints: The two friends find a crate that smells of bananas.
The country is in Central America.
A famous canal between two oceans runs through this country.
questions.fun_fact: In the end the two walk in a circle and land back at their own home, which suddenly seems wonderful to them.

media.credit: JoachimKohler-HB · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: JoachimKohler-HB

questions.description: This heroine has had more “first times” than a whole kindergarten.
questions.question: I wear a red bow in my hair, I have a cat named Mau and a little brother named Jakob. Who am I?
hints: My books are published by Carlsen Verlag.
In my books I learn new things, like riding a bike or swimming.
My name starts with “Con”.
questions.fun_fact: The first Conni picture books came out in the early 1990s.

media.credit: Lauraat · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Lauraat

questions.description: A school with no phone ban, but with suspiciously long ears.
questions.question: Little Red Riding Hood is to the wolf as the bunny children in the picture book “Die Häschenschule” are to which animal?
hints: The bunny teacher warns the children about this enemy.
This animal also likes to sneak up on henhouses at night.
In fables it is often called Reynard.
questions.fun_fact: “Die Häschenschule” (“The Bunny School”) first came out in 1924 and is still in print today.

media.credit: Hextacit · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Hextacit

questions.description: A fairy-tale creature with its own built-in toddler tantrum phase.
questions.question: Who wrote the picture book “Das Neinhorn”, about a unicorn that says no to everything?
hints: He is also a comedian and songwriter.
He wrote books about a kangaroo that moved in with him.
“The Kangaroo Chronicles” are his.
questions.fun_fact: In the Heart Forest, the Neinhorn meets more creatures with pun names, such as the WasBär, the NaHund and the KönigsDochter.

media.credit: OdesaCamp · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: OdesaCamp

questions.description: A magic potion whose name takes two breaths to say.
questions.question: In Michael Ende's “Der Wunschpunsch”, the cat is to the wizard Irrwitzer as which animal is to the witch Tyrannja Vamperl?
hints: The animal is a bird.
In the story it is scruffy, frozen and rather grumpy.
Its name is Jakob Krakel.
questions.fun_fact: The cat Maurizio and Jakob Krakel are secretly spies for the High Council of Animals.

media.credit: Malcolm Lidbury (aka Pinkpasty) · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Malcolm Lidbury (aka Pinkpasty)

questions.description: A sailor whose stories are best taken with a whole bucket of seawater.
questions.question: I'm an old sea dog in a captain's cap. I tell my three grandchildren wild tall tales, and my sailor is called Hein Blöd. Who am I?
hints: The cartoonist Walter Moers created me.
I was often on “Die Sendung mit der Maus.”
My fur is the color of the sea.
questions.fun_fact: In 1999 Walter Moers even wrote a thick novel about him: “Die 13½ Leben des Käpt'n Blaubär” (“The 13½ Lives of Captain Bluebear”).

media.credit: W. Bulach · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: W. Bulach

questions.description: A movie with no screen, no projector and no popcorn crumbs on the couch.
questions.question: With a good audio play, you see everything even though you only listen. Germans call this “Kino im …”, cinema in the what?
hints: The pictures come from your imagination.
It's a part of the body.
It's where your brain is.
questions.fun_fact: The first German radio play was broadcast as early as 1924, long before cassettes existed.

media.credit: Colin · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Colin

questions.description: Two horses, two girls and a farm with more adventures than hay.
questions.question: Bibi rides Sabrina, Tina rides Amadeus. In which decade did the first “Bibi und Tina” cassette come out?
hints: Bibi Blocksberg already had her own audio dramas before that.
Back then, cassettes were still more popular than CDs.
It started shortly after German reunification.
questions.fun_fact: “Bibi und Tina” is a spin-off of “Bibi Blocksberg”, and its first episode came out in 1991.

media.credit: Tahsin A Shah · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Tahsin A Shah

questions.description: A pest controller with a musical instrument and very strict payment terms.
questions.question: The Pied Piper of Hamelin wasn't paid for his work. Who did he then lead out of town with his pipe?
hints: Afterwards, Hamelin was very quiet.
According to the legend, the procession left through a town gate on a summer feast day, June 26, 1284.
According to the legend, 130 of them disappeared.
questions.fun_fact: To this day, no music may be played on Bungelosenstraße in Hamelin, because the procession is said to have gone down that street.

media.credit: Ymblanter · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ymblanter

questions.description: That's an awful lot of pointy tops for just one building.
questions.question: This photo shows part of a famous building in Germany. Which one is it?
hints: It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
It was built from 1248 to 1880, with long breaks.
It stands right next to the train station of a city on the Rhine.
questions.fun_fact: When Cologne Cathedral was finished in 1880, it was the tallest building in the world for a few years.

media.credit: Yair-haklai · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Yair-haklai

questions.description: A bridge that has seen more feet than any shoe store.
questions.question: You walk across the Stone Bridge (Steinerne Brücke) over the Danube in Regensburg. About how old is it?
hints: It is older than the discovery of America.
But the Romans didn't build it.
It was built in the time of knights and the Crusades.
questions.fun_fact: The Wurstkuchl right next to the bridge is said to be one of the oldest sausage kitchens in the world.

media.credit: Lyn Gateley · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Lyn Gateley

questions.description: A poet on the move: boxes full of poems and no moving truck in sight.
questions.question: In 1775, Johann Wolfgang von Goethe moved to Weimar and lived there until he died. In which city was he born?
hints: He only studied in Leipzig and Strasbourg.
The house where he was born is now a museum on the Großer Hirschgraben.
The city has Germany's tallest skyscrapers.
questions.fun_fact: In front of the National Theater in Weimar, Goethe and Schiller stand side by side as a statue, holding one laurel wreath together.

media.credit: Tsungam · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Tsungam

questions.description: Family dinner arguments need a referee, and some referees are made of paper.
questions.question: Atlas is to map as … is to spelling?
hints: In arguments about capital letters, people often quote this book.
The first edition came out in 1880.
You'll find the yellow volume in almost every German classroom.
questions.fun_fact: The first Duden in 1880 had about 27,000 entries; today it has well over 100,000.

media.credit: Shixart1985 · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Shixart1985

questions.fun_fact: Neptune was discovered in 1846 at the Berlin Observatory: Johann Gottfried Galle found it right where Le Verrier had calculated it would be.

media.credit: Michael J. Bennett · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Michael J. Bennett

questions.description: A night light you’d rather not put in a child’s bedroom.
questions.question: It flickers over the moor at night, lures walkers off the safe path, and old legends call it a restless soul. What is it?
hints: Today it is explained by gases rising from the swamp.
If you follow it, you are sure to get lost.
Its German name, Irrlicht, means a light that leads you astray.
questions.fun_fact: Scientists think swamp gases such as methane, catching fire by themselves, are behind the will-o’-the-wisp.

media.credit: erikpaterson · CC BY 2.0 · Flickr via Openverse
media.author: erikpaterson

questions.description: Count turnips out loud around here and you're asking for trouble.
questions.question: According to legend, in which mountain range does the mountain spirit Rübezahl play his tricks?
hints: Today these mountains lie on the border between Poland and the Czech Republic.
Their highest peak is the Schneekoppe.
Their German name fits a spirit of gigantic size.
questions.fun_fact: In the legend, “Rübezahl” was a mocking nickname, and anyone who called him that risked the mountain spirit's anger.

media.credit: Lubor Ferenc · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Lubor Ferenc

questions.description: Here the saying “money doesn't smell” is meant quite literally.
questions.question: I'm an old imperial city that grew rich from silver in my mountain. On my guild house squats a little man who poops out gold coins. Who am I?
hints: I lie on the northern edge of the Harz Mountains.
My Rammelsberg mine is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
My name comes from the little Gose River.
questions.fun_fact: One theory says the Dukatenmännchen on the Kaiserworth house is a reminder of the city's right to mint its own coins.

media.credit: Harz-Seite · CC BY-SA 3.0 de · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Harz-Seite

questions.description: The only garden resident who never has to mow the lawn.
questions.question: This figure with a pointed cap stands in many German gardens. What is it called?
hints: He's pretty small.
He often holds a shovel, a lantern or a wheelbarrow.
In legends, his relatives work deep down in mines.
questions.fun_fact: The first clay garden gnomes were made around 1872 in Gräfenroda in Thuringia.

media.credit: Colibri1968 at English Wikipedia · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Colibri1968 at English Wikipedia

questions.description: A witch's curse that needs no broomstick and no magic wand.
questions.question: It hits suddenly when you bend down or lift something heavy, and people used to think witches shot it at you. Where does a Hexenschuss hurt?
hints: It usually strikes with no warning, after one clumsy move.
Many people find that warmth helps, like a hot-water bottle.
It usually sits low down, just above your bottom.
questions.fun_fact: Doctors call a Hexenschuss “lumbago,” from the Latin word “lumbus,” meaning loin.

media.credit: Raphael Tuck and Sons · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Raphael Tuck and Sons

questions.description: Fairy-tale creatures sadly don't carry ID cards, so you have to recognize them some other way.
questions.question: I don't live in the sea but in rivers and ponds, and I have long hair and a fish tail. Who am I?
hints: I love to sing and comb my hair on the bank.
My sisters in the sea are called mermaids.
My name begins with N.
questions.fun_fact: In old legends, you can spot a nixie who comes on land to dance by the wet hem of her skirt.

media.credit: Toby Hudson · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Toby Hudson

questions.description: A roommate who never pays rent and still knocks everything over.
questions.question: I'm invisible, I slam doors, knock plates off the shelf and rumble through the whole house. Who am I?
hints: Above all, I do one thing: make noise.
I don't live out in nature but with people.

questions.fun_fact: The German word “Poltergeist” was taken into English without any change.

questions.description: A hat that's a lot older than anything in your grandma's closet.
questions.question: You're standing in front of the Imperial Crown, the most important piece of the regalia of the Holy Roman emperors. About how old is it?
hints: It comes from the Middle Ages.
It was probably made in the time of the Ottonian emperors.
It was made around the turn of the first millennium.
questions.fun_fact: For almost 400 years, from 1424 to 1796, the imperial regalia were kept in Nuremberg.

media.author: Bede735c

questions.description: A city that had its moment on the big stage and stayed modest anyway.
questions.question: The Basic Law was proclaimed on May 23, 1949, in the city with this monument. Which city is it?
hints: The city lies on the Rhine.
The monument shows a famous composer who was born here.
For decades it was the capital of West Germany.
questions.fun_fact: In Bonn, the Parliamentary Council met in a former teacher-training college that later became part of the Bundeshaus, the federal parliament building.

media.credit: Dietmar Rabich · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Dietmar Rabich

questions.description: A house that used to be full of nobles and is now full of states.
questions.question: Until 1918, Prussia's noble upper chamber met in this building on Leipziger Straße in Berlin. Today the Bundesrat meets there. What was it first called?
hints: The name tells you who used to get a seat there.
Members got in by birth or were appointed by the king, not elected.
This chamber had no place for ladies.
questions.fun_fact: Its elected counterpart, the Prussian House of Representatives, stands right next door, and Berlin's state parliament meets there today.

media.credit: Flocci Nivis · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Flocci Nivis

questions.description: Giant letters that one emperor spent years steering clear of.

hints: He openly made fun of the new parliament building.
He was a grandson of Britain's Queen Victoria.
He was the last German emperor.
questions.fun_fact: A Berlin family firm cast the bronze letters, supposedly from cannons captured in the wars against Napoleon.

media.credit: Christian Reimer · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Christian Reimer

questions.description: A date whose name Germany had to think about for decades.
questions.question: In 1985, German President Richard von Weizsäcker called May 8 a “day of liberation”. What does this day mark?
questions.answer: The end of World War II in Europe

The founding of the Federal Republic
The end of World War I
hints: Weizsäcker was speaking on the 40th anniversary.
He meant liberation from National Socialism.
On this day, the unconditional surrender of the Wehrmacht took effect.
questions.fun_fact: Berlin made May 8 a one-off public holiday twice: in 2020 and 2025, for the 75th and 80th anniversaries.

media.author: Ziko-C

questions.description: Mail that smells like an election campaign but still isn't junk mail.

hints: You should have enough time to apply for a mail-in vote.
Just a few days ahead would be far too tight for voting by mail.
It's exactly three weeks.
questions.fun_fact: If you lose your polling card, you can still vote: just bring your ID card.

media.credit: Lothar Weber · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Lothar Weber

questions.description: Jewelry you don't buy at a jeweler's: you just pick it off the lawn.

hints: This flower blooms in the lawn almost all year round.

Its English name comes from “day's eye”, because it opens with the morning sun.
questions.fun_fact: Daisies close their flowers at night and when it rains.

media.author: User Ecrips on en.wikipedia

A cyclist on the forest trail
A family with a picnic blanket
hints: It's about something that can burn.
Dry grass and leaves catch fire very quickly.
Someone is about to toast Stockbrot (bread dough on a stick).
questions.fun_fact: In many German states, open fires are banned even up to 100 meters (330 feet) from the edge of a forest.

questions.description: Huge green walls in the fields, and hardly anyone asks who eats all of it.

hints: People eat only a small part of it.
Often the whole plant is chopped into small pieces.
Cows in the barn are happy about it.
questions.fun_fact: A large part of the rest of the corn ends up in biogas plants, where it is turned into electricity.

questions.description: A plant that fights back if you get too close.

hints: It often grows along paths and fences.

Its full English name tells you what it does to your skin.
questions.fun_fact: You can make tea and soup from nettles, and long ago people even made cloth for clothes from them.

media.author: Dominicus Johannes Bergsma

questions.description: A yellow lion that would rather live on the lawn than on the savanna.

hints: Three of these animals eat plants.
One of these animals mostly needs food other than greens.
This pet purrs.
questions.fun_fact: The dandelion got its name from its jagged leaves, which are said to look like lion's teeth (French “dent de lion”).

media.credit: Gerda Arendt · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Gerda Arendt

questions.description: A cake that makes you pull a face at the first bite, out of joy, of course.
questions.question: This cake has shortcrust pastry, a meringue topping and sour, green, slightly hairy berries the size of marbles. Which berries?
hints: These berries grow in many German gardens.
The bush pricks you when you pick them.
Their English name hides a farm bird.
questions.fun_fact: Gooseberries don't only come in green, but also in yellow and even red.

questions.description: A flower that loves to join the summer party in the fields without being invited.

hints: It likes to grow alongside the blue cornflower.

The seeds of its relatives end up on bread rolls.
questions.fun_fact: Its German name, Klatschmohn, probably comes from the clapping sound (“Klatsch”) a petal makes when you slap it on your hand.

They have a cap and a stem.

media.author: Lisalunamorris

In crime shows, it often happens in a bare room with a table.
questions.fun_fact: In real German police work, the official word is usually not “Verhör” but “Vernehmung”.

questions.description: When the street suddenly gets loud and all the cars pull over.
questions.question: Which of these vehicles does NOT drive with blue flashing lights in Germany?
hints: Blue lights are only for vehicles that must get somewhere very fast.
The vehicle you're looking for drives slowly and stops all the time.
It empties the trash cans.
questions.fun_fact: Blue lights have only been required in Germany since 1938; before that, fire trucks mostly warned people with bells.

media.credit: Alexander Scholten · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Alexander Scholten

questions.description: Nervous contestants, stern faces and a man making music with spoons.
questions.question: Whistle is to referee as … is to judge on “Das Supertalent”?
hints: The judges press it with their hand.
When all of them light up red, the act is over.
There's even a golden version of it.
questions.fun_fact: With the golden buzzer, a judge can send an act straight to the final.

media.author: Shixart1985

questions.description: Back then, TV still had a face, and it was the same one every night at eight.
questions.question: From 1959 to 1987 I read the Tagesschau news, for many years as chief newsreader, and people called me “Mister Tagesschau.” Who am I?
hints: I was already reading the Tagesschau in its early years.
In 1987 a colleague took over my post as chief newsreader.
My first name is a double name, and my last name starts with “K.”
questions.fun_fact: Köpcke was the Tagesschau's chief newsreader from 1964 to 1987.

media.credit: electromechanic812291 · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: electromechanic812291

questions.description: One woman, one microphone, and a TV channel that gets a bit more complaint mail afterwards.
questions.question: Which comedian from the Cologne area got her own comedy show on Das Erste, named after her?
hints: Before that, she already had her own satire show on WDR.
She is a huge carnival fan and started her own women's carnival show.
Her last name starts with “K” and is quite unusual.
questions.fun_fact: With “Deine Sitzung”, Kebekus runs a carnival show where almost only women are on stage.

questions.description: Some building sites take even longer than Berlin's new airport, and that's saying something.
questions.question: Three of these Gothic churches only got their towers finished in the 19th century. Which one's tower was already complete in the Middle Ages?

The city sits at the edge of the Black Forest and is known for its “Bächle”, little streams along the streets.
questions.fun_fact: The historian Jacob Burckhardt called it “the most beautiful tower in Christendom”.

media.credit: IanVG · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: IanVG

questions.description: A brick building so red you want to offer it some sunscreen.

Not all of Germany is governed from here, only Berlin itself.
questions.fun_fact: The name “Rotes Rathaus” (Red City Hall) comes from its red clinker bricks, not from politics.

media.credit: Michielverbeek · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Michielverbeek

questions.description: A zoo where the lions are so close you almost want to say hello.
questions.question: In 1907, Carl Hagenbeck opened a zoo in Hamburg with deep moats and fake rocks. What were the moats for?
hints: Before then, zoo animals mostly lived in small cages.
The animals were meant to look like they were in the wild.
The moats are too wide to jump across, so there's no need for cages anymore.
questions.fun_fact: Hagenbeck even patented his idea of enclosures without bars, and zoos around the world copied it.

media.credit: Notafly · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Notafly

questions.description: A polar bear star whose first meals came from a bottle.
questions.question: Knut the polar bear was born in December 2006 and became world-famous. How much did he weigh at birth?
hints: Polar bear cubs are born blind and almost hairless.
Adult polar bears weigh hundreds of kilos, but their babies are tiny.
Knut weighed less than a small bag of flour.
questions.fun_fact: Zookeeper Thomas Dörflein raised Knut with a bottle because his mother didn't take care of him.

media.credit: Adam Bishop · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Adam Bishop

questions.description: A building that clearly doesn't feel like touching the ground.
questions.question: The exhibition building of the Porsche Museum in Stuttgart seems to float. How many supports does it rest on?
hints: There's a big open square under the building.
There are surprisingly few supports.
There are fewer supports than a normal table has legs.
questions.fun_fact: The Porsche Museum in Stuttgart-Zuffenhausen opened in 2009.

media.credit: Rolf Kranz · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Rolf Kranz

questions.description: A piece of headwear that gets argued about before every bike ride.
questions.question: You wear it on your head when cycling, it has air holes and a strap under the chin. What is it for?
questions.answer: It protects your head in a fall
wrong_answers: It keeps your hair nice and tidy
It makes the bike go faster
hints: In many families, kids have to put it on before they're allowed to ride off.
It's soft on the inside and hard on the outside.
When you fall over, you're glad you had it on.
questions.fun_fact: After a crash you should replace a bike helmet, even if you can't see any damage on the outside.

wrong_answers: The next traffic light turns red
hints: The box has taken a photo.
It comes a few days or weeks later.
It lands in your mailbox with bad news.
questions.fun_fact: Many speed cameras use infrared light, so you can barely see the flash, or not at all.

questions.description: City traffic: someone's honking here, someone's been hunting for a parking spot for twenty minutes there.

hints: You often find me in narrow lanes in an old town.
Cyclists are sometimes still allowed to ride the other way.
My name has the number one in it.
questions.fun_fact: In many German cities, cyclists may ride the wrong way down a one-way street if an extra sign allows it.

questions.description: When a car won't wake up in the morning, it needs a cup of coffee from the car next door.

hints: It's much more than a small battery for the remote control.
It's much less than a wall socket.
The number is a dozen.
questions.fun_fact: When jump-starting, the red cable always goes on the plus terminal, and the black one on the minus terminal or on bare metal on the engine.

questions.description: A train station that loves stacking things as much as a kid with building blocks.

One line runs up high, the other deep underground.
One direction is east–west, the other north–south.

media.author: Martin Falbisoner

hints: The rule applies in the front and in the back.

Don't forget to count yourself!
questions.fun_fact: In Germany, wearing a seat belt in the front became the law in 1976, but you only got fined for skipping it starting in 1984.

media.author: Santeri Viinamäki

Soon afterwards, many move on to a secondary school.
questions.fun_fact: For the cycling test, children often practice with the police at a children's traffic training ground (Jugendverkehrsschule).

media.author: Herzi Pinki

To measure how fast cars are going
hints: It's about safety.
You often find it on bridges and in sharp curves, too.
Its German name, Leitplanke, says that it “guides” cars.
questions.fun_fact: Guardrails are built to bend when a car hits them, soaking up part of the force of the crash.

Only the front ones are in the air.
It's the two back wheels.
questions.fun_fact: Some tow trucks have a bed that tilts, so the whole car can be pulled up onto it.

media.author: Lynxano

questions.description: One letter that gets millions of commuters to work on time every morning (usually).
questions.question: It runs in Berlin, Hamburg and Munich, and its sign is blue with a white letter. What does the “U” in U-Bahn stand for?
hints: It has to do with where it mostly runs.

It mostly runs through tunnels beneath the streets.

Shovels, a foundation and the grounds of a brass works.

He has the same first name as Mozart.

My nickname claims I could bend horseshoes with my bare hands.
questions.fun_fact: The porcelain factory stayed in the Albrechtsburg for over 150 years, until it moved to a new building in 1863.

My invention is called lithography, meaning “stone writing.”

media.author: Edinburgh City of Print

Siegfried Lenz's novel “The German Lesson” tells of a painter who recalls me.

This form of rule is the opposite of democracy and has no king.
